#5400. AI Can Build Your Product in a Day —Here’s How Founders Get Someone to Actually Pay for It

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Lessons from 500 first-time founders on how they landed their first paying customer, and how they built momentum.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

This summer, more than 500 people from more than 50 countries joined an eight-week startup camp my company runs. Most had never started a business. Many had never written a line of code, and it didn’t matter. With today’s AI tools, most of them had a working product within the first couple of weeks.

Getting someone to pay was the hard part, and about 1 in 10 managed it.

I spent the weeks after camp asking those founders how they did it. This is what I learned:

Almost none of the first customers were strangers. One founder, a marketing consultant, built a small ad tool for his own use. He showed it to a group of entrepreneurs he met with regularly because he thought it might help them. Those 10 became the first paying customers. Another founder built a language-learning app. Her first customer was a math teacher in Italy, the friend of a friend of a friend. Three introductions away sounds far, but each one carried a little trust, and that was enough.

If you are starting out, write down the 50 people who would take your call. Your first customer is more likely on that list than in an ad audience.

The founders who got paid often sold something that wasn’t really a product yet. A founder working on grief support ran her whole service through Instagram direct messages. She had more than 500 conversations before she built a website, and each conversation was both the product and the demo.

The language app founder did something similar. She got her first user on a video call, set her up personally, and promised to build what she needed. The customer bought an annual plan.

AI makes it tempting to build first because building is so easy now. But a working app doesn’t prove anyone wants it. A person paying for the rough version does. Find the smallest version of your core promise and start figuring out whether someone will pay for that.

I didn’t find a single founder whose first sale came from a stranger on a checkout page alone. The yes came from a text message, a phone call, a video call or showing up in person. One founder who used to run a car collision repair shop found that ads, websites and email never closed a sale for him. Knocking on doors and picking up the phone did. Funnels matter later. For the first customer, you are the funnel.

Many founders put their first few hundred dollars into social media ads. Most learned the same lesson: ads buy attention, not trust. One founder got more than 40 signups and zero buyers. The grief-support founder got clicks and traffic but no customers, because someone scrolling past an ad on a random Tuesday is not someone who needs help right now.

There was one clear exception. A founder with a golf swing app got his first customers through paid ads. My read is that golfers already know they have the problem and go looking for a fix. When your buyer already knows they have the problem, ads can work. When they don’t, you are paying to explain the problem and the product at the same time.

Sometimes the first sale is for something you didn’t mean to sell. The marketing consultant set out to build one business. The side tool he made for himself became the business. Slack was created the same way – as an internal tool in what used to be a gaming company. The former collision shop owner had a lesson from his old business that stuck with me. He closed about 90% of the people who came in, and he was never the cheapest. Many of them didn’t really want the repair. They wanted the insurance money from the claim, and he helped them get what they actually needed. Early conversations will tell you what people will pay for if you listen for what is implied, not just what is said.

AI has taken most of the cost out of building. What it hasn’t changed is that someone has to decide to trust you with their money. That’s why the first $100 matters far more than the amount. It’s the first proof that someone who owes you nothing values what you offer.

So before you build the next feature, ask a different question: Who already trusts me, and what could I sell them this week?

Building is nearly free. Being trusted is not.

#5399. A Country Club Built Around a Private Racetrack? Why Exclusive Experiences are the Biggest Trend Among The Wealthy

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

APEX Motorclub is a private motorsports club in Maricopa, Arizona, on a 280-acre facility with race tracks, skid pads and luxury trackside condos, and by offering lifetime memberships to families it taps into the wealthy’s growing interest in passing down passions, not just assets.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Country clubs are an American tradition among those wealthy enough to afford them. But as unique experiences become increasingly coveted, many members are looking for more exciting alternatives to a golf course and some fancy hors d’oeuvres. Enter Apex Motor Club.

APEX Motor Club is a private motorsports club in Maricopa, Arizona, built around cars, community and competition.

As President Bill Barba puts it, “We’re similar to a country club, but instead of golf courses, we have race tracks.”

The Club is a 280-acre facility featuring 2 race tracks, a six-acre skid pad, 96 trackside garage condos, a drivers’ lounge and a clubhouse.

The goal is to give motorsports enthusiasts a place to share that passion with others, including their family members. At the same time, the exclusive luxury landscape offers an escape from the pressure of running a billion-dollar company, as some of its members do.

“We’ve got members whose names are known,” Barba says. “They run global companies, plus some local entrepreneurs that built great businesses. Motorsports are interesting because they all share the joy, rather than expecting to be Mr. or Mrs. So and So when they’re out here. That’s part of the culture we’ve created.”

There are two primary membership types: Gold, a $70,000 initiation fee plus an annual $8,000 fee and Platinum, a $90,000 initiation fee plus an annual $15,000 fee. The two are similar, offering 240+ annual track days, transferable membership and family access, with Platinum offering event host days. They also recently introduced a one-year membership for $35,000 and an under-35 membership with a $25,000 initiation fee plus $4,500 annually.

“Motorsports is not a cheap endeavor,” Barba explains. “To run a car for a weekend out here, you go through tires, brakes and maintenance. Depending on the type of car, that cost can go up quite a bit.”

While APEX provides the location and platform, members must maintain their own cars. Some have small teams doing only the necessary maintenance, while others come to the track with five people analyzing the data behind each lap. Some look to shave milliseconds off their cornering, while others just want a place to let the fancy ride they just bought rip.

APEX’s business model includes partnerships with luxury car companies. They have a deal with Lexus, which brought out cars to join the APEX fleet. They also have a relationship with Aston Martin, which has an on-site presence in their garage condos. The local McLaren Scottsdale, one of the country’s highest-volume McLaren dealers, is a corporate member of the club.

Companies will also rent the tracks for events, including Ferrari, Mercedes and Porsche.

“It gives them a chance to put people who aren’t necessarily enthusiastic enough to join a club on a track to understand what the car can do,” Barba explains. According to him, 85% of the engineering in performance cars never shows up on the street. At APEX, someone might own their fourth Porsche 911 but never experience its full power until they get on the course with an instructor.

“The guy who buys or leases a Lamborghini to park at the valet is not a member of a motorsports club,” Barba says. “Our members tend to have more enthusiasm for the vehicles. Then there’s a whole different area of what level of racing they may want.”

While most members are interested in track time, Barba estimates about 20% take wheel-to-wheel racing seriously. For them, APEX runs an 11-race series with 10 to 25 people per race, depending on the car. “Some people love it and thrive on the competition and pushing the car. Others want to enjoy the tracking and their times, but not race,” Babra says.

What sets APEX apart from the competition is its family policy.

“If you join APEX, your spouse and kids are a part of it, and we don’t age them out,” Barba shares. “What we saw historically was that a lot of clubs would age kids out, and then they’d have to buy a membership. We want kids to stay as long as possible because it keeps parents, grandparents and everyone else engaged. So it’s a family membership because we want it to be a family experience.”

This plays into a larger theme among the wealthy: finding the “new inheritance.” Rather than passing down expensive paintings and big houses, rich parents want to give their kids something more meaningful and personal.

One option is their passions. “Members will talk about the first race car they had, the first time they reached a certain speed, or the first time they watched their child drive a car,” Barba says. “It’s a passion that passes down, and it connects back to what I believe is most potent about motorsports: the emotions.”

One example is the Bacon family. Seth Bacon had built a successful logistics business focused on organ donations and sold it. Looking for a way to spend more time with his teenage son Jace as he approached adulthood, he found an unexpected solution: racing.

“He was about to turn 16 and get his driver’s license. He’s getting a job. He was busy in school. He’s about to go off to college, and I thought this is that period where he’s beginning to separate himself from the nest,” Seth says. “I wanted an opportunity for us to still do something tight together.”

The two visited APEX to watch a few races. Before long, they bought a pair of Radical race cars and hit the track themselves.

“Instead of the son ignoring him at 16, they’re working together on racing,” Barba says with a laugh.

At Jace’s first race at another club in Nevada, father and son competed together, with Jace winning.

“It made a real impact on the dad that out there, his son is an equal with guys who are running billion-dollar companies,” Barba says.

The Bacons could take their cars to any track, but few offer the built-in community they’ve found at APEX.

“There’s a lot of senior drivers, a lot of retired professional drivers who are members there, and everywhere we go, they’re always checking in on him, asking about his career,” Seth says of Jace. “It really is more of a community of people who are willing to support one another, not only on track, but also, how did that business of yours go? Did you get that acquisition you were looking for? What do you need next?”

Business connections are great, but at the end of the day, APEX is about cars, community and competition. A hole-in-one is unforgettable, but the average day on the golf course doesn’t necessarily make the lifetime highlight reel. Driving a luxury race car at breakneck speeds on an open track? That’s an experience that’s not only incredible, but repeatable.

Country clubs are an American tradition among those wealthy enough to afford them. But as unique experiences become increasingly coveted, many members are looking for more exciting alternatives to a golf course and some fancy hors d’oeuvres. Enter Apex Motor Club.

APEX Motor Club is a private motorsports club in Maricopa, Arizona, built around cars, community and competition.

As President Bill Barba puts it, “We’re similar to a country club, but instead of golf courses, we have race tracks.”

#5398. Coding Dojo co-founder unveils ‘Idea to Launch,’ a 30-day program to help aspiring founders build with AI

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 29, 2026 at 8:00 amOctober 29, 2026 at 7:47 am

Richard Wang, co-founder and former CEO of coding bootcamp Coding Dojo, is launching Idea to Launch, a 30-day program that helps would-be founders turn a startup idea into a working product using AI coding tools and hands-on engineering help.

Nearly four years after selling Coding Dojo to Perdoceo for $70 million, Wang was looking for a way to keep doing work that had a measurable impact on people’s lives. He found it in mentoring aspiring founders.

Wang thinks AI is about to do for software what smartphones did for video. Cheap cameras and cloud platforms gave rise to the influencer economy, and he believes AI will push the cost of building a product close to zero.

“We’re going to create this whole new builder economy that’s about to come in the next three to five years,” he said. “Baby boomers are gifted with cheap housing. I think Gen Z is going to be gifted with a cheap price to build.”

He sees plenty of demand. Citing a Shopify-Gallup study and a Zapier/Harris poll, Idea to Launch says 60% of Americans have a business idea but only 9% launch one. Wang said the reasons people hold back include fear of failure, not knowing how to get started, and not wanting to give up a paycheck or benefits.

Unlike accelerators such as Techstars or Y Combinator, Idea to Launch doesn’t take equity, and participants don’t have to quit their jobs. Over 10 evening sessions, founders get coaching, run customer interviews, build a product with AI tools such as Lovable, Replit and Cursor, and plan a launch. Each founder also gets 10 hours of one-on-one help from professional engineers.

Wang said people without technical backgrounds can now vibe-code 80% to 90% of a product on their own. The hard part, he said, is connecting it to other services, setting up the database correctly and making it secure.

“We’ll provide that type of knowledge with real engineering support,” he said. For engineers who have never done customer discovery or marketing, the program fills in the business side.

Security researchers have found serious vulnerabilities in apps built on vibe-coding platforms. A 2025 scan found 170 of 1,645 apps built with Lovable exposing user data, and another case this year exposed nearly 19,000 user records. Wang said the program’s engineers will make sure security holes are fixed “before they launch or before they get onto the first customer.”

The first cohort starts Jan. 11, followed by three more through April. Each is capped at 15 to 20 founders. Tuition is $3,500 for the inaugural cohort, down from the normal $5,000. Sessions will be held in person in Seattle or Bellevue, and Wang said he expects to pick a space within the next month. He is self-funding the venture.

Wang, who immigrated from China at 13 and was the first in his family to attend college, became Coding Dojo’s CEO in 2015. He left in 2017 for Trupanion and returned in 2019. The company grew to $50 million in peak annual revenue, according to Wang, and had 194 employees at the time of the sale, according to GeekWire’s earlier reporting. It operated campuses in several states before shifting online during the pandemic.

Wang sees Idea to Launch expanding to other tech hubs, then online, and eventually licensing the program globally, much as Coding Dojo grew to multiple campuses. If the first cohorts go well, he can envision a follow-up program, Launch to Traction, to help founders find more customers.

He doesn’t plan to invest in participants’ companies. Having spent years building and selling Coding Dojo, Wang said he knows how hard that road is and would rather “cheer them on from the sidelines.” He said taking VC money at Coding Dojo created pressure to grow 100% a year, something he calls “startup steroids.”

For Wang, the point isn’t to find the next unicorn. It’s to give more people a shot at building something now that AI has made it cheaper and easier.

“I think everyone should try at least once just to bring their idea to reality,” he said.

#5397. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5396. 4 Reasons Your Homepage Messaging Isn’t Converting (and How to Address Them)

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Why isn’t your homepage converting visitors into customers? Discover four common website messaging mistakes and how customer interviews can help fix them.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Your homepage has one of the most important jobs in marketing: convincing the right visitors that your solution is worth exploring.

Yet many companies struggle to turn website traffic into demos, trials or purchases. They invest in SEO, advertising and content to attract visitors, only to watch most of them leave without taking action.

Having spent more than a decade helping B2B companies improve their messaging as a product marketing executive and consultant, I’ve learned that the problem often starts with a misunderstanding of what buyers need to hear before they’re willing to take the next step.

Companies often explain their products from their own perspective. They highlight what they’ve built, everything their product can do and the benefits they assume customers care about. It often results in messaging like “The AI-native GTM platform powering Precision GTM at scale.”

But buyers have their own priorities, frustrations and concerns. If your homepage doesn’t address those, even a great product can struggle to convert.

Here are four common messaging mistakes and how to fix them.

Many companies want their homepage to communicate everything their product can do. They try to capture multiple use cases, features and benefits in a single headline, hoping to appeal to as many potential customers as possible.

The result is often vague messaging that promises to “streamline operations,” “boost productivity,” “help your business grow,” or vague slogans like “We’ll take care of your accounting so you can focus on your business.”

These statements may have some truth, but they’re unlikely to resonate with someone facing a specific, urgent problem. When you try to communicate everything, you risk saying nothing compelling enough to make a buyer act.

Consider a project management platform for marketing agencies. Its homepage might promise to “streamline projects and improve team productivity” or some version of that. But customer interviews could reveal that agency owners are particularly frustrated by missed deadlines that damage client relationships.

Now the company has a more specific message to lead with: “Deliver every client project on time, without constantly chasing your team for updates.”

That message is more likely to capture the attention of an agency owner who’s tired of apologizing to clients for late work. It connects with a problem they’re experiencing and have a reason to solve.

In my customer research work, I often find that what companies think customers value most differs from what actually motivates them to look for a solution.

To find your strongest message, interview recent customers or prospects. Ask what prompted them to start looking for a solution, what problem they were most eager to solve and why solving it became a priority.

Look for the single problem or desired outcome that most consistently motivates your ideal customers to act. Lead with that message on your homepage. You can use the rest of the page to communicate everything else your product offers.

Your biggest competitor isn’t always another company. Often, it’s the way your prospective customers already do things.

They might recognize the problem your product solves but have learned to live with it. Unless the cost of continuing becomes clear, they have little reason to make a change.

Imagine a software product that automates invoicing for agencies. Its homepage might say, “Automate invoicing and save time.” That’s a reasonable benefit, but it doesn’t fully communicate why the problem deserves attention.

Now consider the agency owner’s existing workflow. Project managers finish work, someone manually checks billable hours, invoices are created at the end of the month, and the finance team follows up on unpaid balances.

The consequences might include delayed invoices, missed billable work, slower payments and unnecessary administrative costs. These are much more compelling reasons to change.

Instead of simply promising automation, the homepage could explain how manual billing creates revenue leakage and cash flow problems.

To make the status quo feel costly, make its consequences visible.

Ask customers what happened before they adopted your solution. How much time did they spend on the problem? What mistakes occurred? What opportunities did they miss? What happened when they delayed fixing it?

Use their answers to communicate the business and emotional impact of the problem. Wherever possible, include real numbers, concrete examples and real-life anecdotes.

Even when visitors recognize the problem, they still need to understand how your solution will improve their situation.

Many homepages fall short here because they emphasize generic benefits or product capabilities without explaining how the product fits into the buyer’s actual workflow.

For example, an AI-powered customer support platform might highlight advanced language models, intelligent routing and automated workflows. But customer research might reveal that support managers primarily want to reduce the number of repetitive tickets their agents handle without compromising customer satisfaction.

They want to know which questions AI can resolve, when a human agent takes over and how the platform will connect with their existing help desk. The homepage should answer those deeper questions or help the reader easily find that guidance elsewhere on the website.

Rather than simply stating that the product “improves support efficiency,” it could walk visitors through a familiar scenario: A customer asks about an order, AI retrieves the relevant information, and the issue gets resolved without an agent getting involved.

A simple workflow illustration can make the value immediately understandable.

I’ve found that understanding a customer’s existing process is one of the most useful parts of customer interviews. It reveals not only which benefits matter but also which details buyers need to see before they can imagine using a product.

Ask customers to walk you through how they handled the problem before finding your solution and what changed afterward. Then build your messaging around those specific improvements.

Even when buyers see the value, they might hesitate because they’re uncertain about what happens next.

Will the product work for their business? Will implementation be difficult? Will their team actually use it? Can they trust your company to deliver? These concerns can prevent otherwise interested visitors from converting.

I frequently see websites use customer logos and testimonials as their main form of reassurance. Those elements help, but they don’t necessarily answer the specific questions making buyers hesitate.

A small business considering a new accounting platform, for example, might be far more concerned about migrating its financial data than whether the software has won an industry award.

Showing how migration works, explaining the support available and featuring a customer who successfully made the switch could do more to increase conversions.

The most effective reassurance addresses the risks your buyers actually perceive.

Interview customers about the concerns they had before purchasing. Ask what nearly stopped them, what reassured them and what information would have made their decision easier.

Use those insights to select the right customer stories, product demonstrations, guarantees, implementation details and FAQs for your homepage.

Improving homepage conversions doesn’t always require a complete redesign, more persuasive copywriting or another round of A/B testing. Sometimes, the most valuable starting point is a handful of conversations with recent buyers.

Ask what problem made them look for a solution, why they couldn’t continue with their existing approach, what convinced them your product was right and what almost prevented them from buying.

Their answers can help you build a homepage that speaks to a real priority, makes the cost of inaction clear, demonstrates relevant value and gives visitors the confidence to take the next step.

That’s a much stronger foundation for conversion than guessing which headline or call to action might perform better.

Your homepage has one of the most important jobs in marketing: convincing the right visitors that your solution is worth exploring.

Yet many companies struggle to turn website traffic into demos, trials or purchases. They invest in SEO, advertising and content to attract visitors, only to watch most of them leave without taking action.

Having spent more than a decade helping B2B companies improve their messaging as a product marketing executive and consultant, I’ve learned that the problem often starts with a misunderstanding of what buyers need to hear before they’re willing to take the next step.

#5395. AWS growth hits 39%, its fastest in nearly five years, as Amazon misses on earnings

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 1:37 pmOctober 30, 2026 at 10:35 am

Amazon Web Services revenue grew 39% to $46 billion in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said he expects the cloud unit to top 40% growth in both 2027 and 2028.

That wasn’t enough for investors. Amazon posted earnings of $1.89 per share, well short of the $1.97 analysts expected, as higher interest costs on its growing debt and other losses ate into its profit.

Operating income beat expectations at $28.1 billion, above the high end of Amazon’s own guidance, and the 13.9% operating margin for the quarter was the highest in the company’s history.

Revenue of $201.9 billion, up 12%, came in just under analyst estimates but at the top of Amazon’s forecast range. Shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading, after closing down 4% during the regular session.

Update: On the earnings call, Jassy said AWS has a backlog of $578 billion in contracted future revenue, more than double a year earlier. He also said Amazon expects to spend “meaningfully more” on capital projects in 2027 than the roughly $220 billion it plans for this year.

Amazon may need to count on its legendary willingness to be “misunderstood for long periods of time,” as it asks investors to look past the costs to where its biggest businesses are headed.

In the company’s earnings release, Jassy said Amazon’s retail business is gaining market share with improving margins. Retail sales, including online stores, physical stores and third-party seller services, totaled nearly $500 billion over the past 12 months, and AWS is now at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate.

“There has never been a trillion dollar revenue business, and we may have two of them in the next 5-10 years,” he said.

On the earnings call, Jassy said those two businesses are AWS and Amazon’s stores business.

Advertising grew 11% to $19.6 billion, or 12% excluding currency changes, down from 22% on that basis a year earlier. Amazon blamed the timing of Prime Day and a few other factors, and said it expects ad growth to return to the high teens in the fourth quarter.

Online stores grew 2% to $68.5 billion, held back by Prime Day moving into the second quarter this year. Amazon said overall revenue growth would have been about 4 percentage points higher without the shift.

Third-party seller services, the fees Amazon collects from merchants on its site, grew 9% to $46.5 billion. AWS came within about $500 million of it.

Subscription services, which includes Prime memberships, grew 11% to $14 billion.

Physical stores, mostly Whole Foods, grew 2% to $5.7 billion.

Outlook: Amazon expects fourth-quarter revenue of $240 billion to $247 billion, up 12% to 16%, and operating income of $28.5 billion to $33.5 billion.

Amazon CFO Brian Olsavsky said on the earnings call that costs for Amazon Leo, the company’s satellite internet service, are weighing on its fourth-quarter profit forecast as the service gets ready to launch later this year.

Wall Street had expected fourth-quarter operating income of $33.2 billion, near the top of that range, according to analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives. It still expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year.

Amazon’s free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier, mostly because of its AI investments.

#5394. XRP Ledger Foundation Adds Flare to Validator List

The XRP Ledger Foundation has added Flare Networks to its list of recommended validators, increasing its involvement in the consensus and governance of the XRP Ledger.

On Oct. 28, the XRP Ledger Foundation took to X to reveal that it had added Flare to its list of recommended validators. They highlighted Flare's dedication to the XRP Ledger ecosystem.

"We welcome @FlareNetworks to the recommended XRP Ledger validator list," the Foundation revealed.

The Foundation detailed Flare's alignment with the core values of the network. It revealed how the project actively engages in governance and participates in the XRP ecosystem as a whole.

Flare responded to the news, expressing its gratitude to the Foundation and those who openly reviewed its application.

Flare rolled out FXRP on its mainnet in September 2025. FXRP lets XRP holders benefit from decentralized finance using Flare's infrastructure (FAssets) for XRP.

Validators are important for the security and stability of the XRP Ledger.

The XRP Ledger doesn't use a proof-of-work mining system as Bitcoin does. Instead, it has its own consensus mechanism for confirming the validity and order of transactions.

Validators independently interact with each other and agree on which transactions should be part of the new version of the ledger. This prevents double-spending and helps participants maintain a consistent version of the transactions.

Not all validators are equally influential in reaching a consensus.

XRPL servers have a Unique Node List (UNL) of validators they trust. A server administrator can set up its own list, but many choose to follow the recommended list of validators published by the XRP Ledger Foundation and Ripple.

This is why being included in the Foundation's recommended list is quite significant. It means the validator is seen as a reliable and independent one.

The XRP Ledger's recommended validator list includes cryptocurrency firms, independent infrastructure providers, and universities.

Some of the notable names include Ripple, XRPL Labs, Bithomp, GateHub, Peersyst Technology, and XRPL Commons.

There are also some universities such as the University of Kansas, the Australian National University, and the University of Nicosia (among others).

#5393. The Systems Behind Your Business Are Changing Beneath the Surface — and Most Teams Haven’t Caught On

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The GTM stack is getting an operating system. Most teams don’t know they’re already building on it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Over the past two years, a subtle transformation has taken place in how go-to-market technology gets constructed, yet most executive teams have not given a name to what they are actually building.

If you audit a modern revenue organization, you will likely find five or six separate systems querying the exact same data source in the background: lead scoring, automated routing, territory assignment, enrichment steps in marketing automation and AI SDRs pulling context before drafting outreach. And what matters is that none of these workflows require a human operator to log into a browser tab or export a spreadsheet.

When multiple systems continuously query a single data source to execute automated tasks unattended, that source has stopped being a software tool. It has become infrastructure — the operating system underneath your revenue stack.

The transition from a point tool to an operating system is rarely a deliberate procurement decision. It happens quietly through a change in operational direction.

A software tool answers a question a human explicitly asked. Core infrastructure answers questions nobody asked, on an automated schedule, without human intervention. When an account executive opens a research tab at 2 p.m. to look up a prospect, they are using a tool. When an automated routing engine queries the same data layer at 2 a.m. to assign an incoming lead based on parent-subsidiary hierarchy and buying signals, that system is running on an operating system.

The simplest way to determine whether a data source has become your stack’s operating system is to examine your failure modes. If that provider goes dark for a week and a few reps lose a research portal, you are using a tool. But if lead scoring drifts, routing rules misfire and automated workflows stall, your organization is running on infrastructure.

For technical builders evaluating their stack architecture today, the critical challenge is avoiding misclassification. Treating infrastructure like a temporary tool leads to casual vendor swaps that break workflows across your ecosystem. On the flip side, treating a basic tool like infrastructure causes you to overpay for software you could easily swap over a weekend.

To determine what you actually hold, run a simple diagnostic: Price the divorce, not the contract.

Instead of reviewing the renewal invoice, write the actual engineering migration plan required to replace your current data provider. Map every workflow that reads from the layer, every AI agent that pulls its fields into context, every scoring algorithm trained on its records and every downstream system storing copies of its truth. Then, estimate the cost of rewiring those connections in engineering quarters rather than software license dollars.

If replacing the provider means simply swapping user logins, you own a tool. If replacing it requires re-architecting how your systems communicate, you have built an operating system.

When an intelligence layer moves underneath the stack, its core function changes. It stops serving up individual contact lookups to human users and starts performing continuous, unattended background operations.

At the center of that is entity resolution: resolving a CRM record, a web form fill and an attendee on a sales call to the same human and ultimate parent company. It handles corporate hierarchy mapping, ensuring automated agents do not prospect a subsidiary while a strategic enterprise team negotiates with the parent holding company. It constantly maps call transcripts, CRM stage changes and external intent signals onto a single, unified record.

We ran this exact transition internally when I stepped into the CMO seat at ZoomInfo. Rather than making external claims, our first move was instrumenting our own marketing organization directly on our platform — wiring scoring, routing, signal-driven plays and AI workflows into one shared context graph.

The immediate lesson was that an operating system requires uncompromising identity resolution first. Automated workflows built on top of fragmented records or stale lists do not create efficiency; they simply distribute confusion at scale. When an AI agent acts unattended, every field requires clear data provenance, accompanied by strict low-confidence rules: If a record is ambiguous, route it to a human, log the exception, and pause execution.

You can copy a stack in a quarter, but you can’t copy three years of context. The gap between organizations that treat data as a point tool and those that build on an underlying operating system becomes impossible to close quickly.

That compounding advantage manifests across two operational dimensions: velocity from signal to touch and marginal unit economics. When a key champion changes jobs, an agentic workflow wired into an intelligence layer catches the movement, links the executive to historical relationship context and routes a relevant touchpoint the same day. On an operating system, every new workflow you build becomes cheaper than the last because the underlying integration logic already exists.

In an AI-native ecosystem, basic contact records are rapidly commoditizing. Long-term defensibility belongs to the continuous, authoritative data graph underneath — the operating system that every agent and workflow defaults to by design.

Over the past two years, a subtle transformation has taken place in how go-to-market technology gets constructed, yet most executive teams have not given a name to what they are actually building.

If you audit a modern revenue organization, you will likely find five or six separate systems querying the exact same data source in the background: lead scoring, automated routing, territory assignment, enrichment steps in marketing automation and AI SDRs pulling context before drafting outreach. And what matters is that none of these workflows require a human operator to log into a browser tab or export a spreadsheet.

When multiple systems continuously query a single data source to execute automated tasks unattended, that source has stopped being a software tool. It has become infrastructure — the operating system underneath your revenue stack.

Before joining Discovery, Saxena was with Amazon for 19 years over two stints, most recently as vice president of technology for Amazon Marketplace. He also held leadership roles at Microsoft and internet infrastructure startups.

Tyler Whitworth is stepping down as executive vice president and chief product officer for WBD’s streaming business. “Leo brings a unique blend of vision, relationships, and entrepreneurship experience,” the organization said, noting his background as a wildland firefighter, startup founder and patent holder for wearable safety gear.

Abiodun’s accomplishments include co-creating the Seattle Climate Innovation Hub, launching the Opalene Climate Challenge and helping lead the Just Future Climate Labs initiative.

#5390. Garlinghouse: 2026 Is Phenomenal Year for Ripple

Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse has called 2026 a "phenomenal" year for the company as it witnesses a significant increase in transaction volumes and business activities.

The Ripple boss has emphasized that the company has witnessed a huge surge in its transaction volumes in the last year, showing the rising demand for its blockchain-based financial infrastructure.

Garlinghouse further reiterated his big plans for XRP as he foresees the crypto eventually becoming an institutional gold standard for crypto payment rails.

Nevertheless, Garlinghouse admitted that XRP may not necessarily be ideal for all financial transactions.

Garlinghouse is clear that Ripple will continue to focus on XRP for cases where the crypto is clearly advantageous.

He stated that it makes good business sense for the company.

Garlinghouse argues that XRP doesn't necessarily need to be the solution for all the transactions that happen on Ripple's infrastructure to be commercially viable.

"We think that XRP is very efficient in some use cases. Probably not in other use cases. But that's ok," he said.

The Ripple CEO is more than okay with XRP being utilized for a small portion of customer transactions.

"That's great. That still means that I am getting some of the pie," he added.

"Sometimes I think people get a little fixated on how big the piece is and how big the pie is," he added.

With his remarks, Garlinghouse seems to suggest that Ripple's approach with XRP is a very pragmatic one. The company is focused on growing its business and finding cases where XRP can be truly beneficial.

Meanwhile, David Schwartz, Ripple's CTO emeritus and one of the co-creators of the XRP Ledger, has made a bold prediction for the future of blockchain technology.

Schwartz was asked about where he sees XRP and Ripple in 5 years. Schwartz sees mass retail adoption ahead.

Schwartz also foresees blockchain technology being just as prevalent and fundamental to life as the internet.

Garlinghouse's positive outlook comes as Ripple is celebrating the 10th edition of its biggest event — the Swell conference in New York City from Oct. 27–29.

A lot of announcements have already come out of the event, showcasing Ripple's growing ambitions in the institutional finance sphere.

The big one includes U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's appearance. He sat down with Garlinghouse to talk about the future of digital assets and the American financial system.

Ripple also announced a big partnership with Robinhood to bring more RLUSD stablecoin and infrastructure use cases. The partnership focuses on institutional settlement, prime brokerage, and treasury use cases.

The company also deepened its relationship with the banking giant BNY. The expanded collaboration includes digital asset custody and tokenized trade finance using XRP, RLUSD, and the XRP Ledger.

Also, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency finally approved Ripple National Trust Bank's last regulatory hurdle.

On top of that, Coinbase has agreed to bring more RLUSD availability to the exchange's retail and institutional platforms.

All the announcements come with impressive growth numbers that Ripple has shared.

Per the company, Ripple is on its way to ending 2026 with roughly $900M in annualized product revenue. Also, Ripple has reported a 3x increase in the number of customers and partners that are using multiple products from Ripple's expanding product line.

The company's financial infrastructure is used by over 1,700 institutions, corporations, and enterprises.

With all the developments, it's no surprise that Garlinghouse is particularly bullish on Ripple's future as the company tries to carve out its spot in a rapidly changing financial services landscape.

#5389. A Next-Day ‘Thank You’ Can Do More for Your Career Than You Think

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

When someone gives you a gift, extends a favor or considers you for an opportunity, take the time to recognize their effort.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The business world presents countless opportunities to make positive impressions that can influence your career trajectory. Whether you receive a thoughtful gift, benefit from a professional favor or interview for a new position, knowing when and how to express appreciation is an important professional skill.

Unfortunately, not everyone recognizes these moments for what they are: opportunities to demonstrate character, emotional intelligence and respect for others.

In my experience as a business owner, you can rarely go wrong by showing gratitude. A sincere thank-you email or text sent within 24 hours can distinguish you from colleagues and competitors who overlook this simple courtesy.

Here are three situations when a next-day thank-you can make a meaningful difference.

As a business owner, I often give team members tickets to concerts, theatrical performances or sporting events. Whenever possible, I personalize these gifts. For example, if I know an employee follows a particular sports team, I may offer tickets to see that team play.

Naturally, I appreciate the initial thank you. That acknowledgment usually arrives through our in-office chat tool shortly after the employee receives my offer.

When an employee sends a follow-up text or email after attending the event, especially one that includes a photo or personal detail, it tells me something important about that person’s character.

Employees often share how exciting the final minutes of the game were or mention that the concert exceeded expectations. These details show that the gift was genuinely appreciated.

More importantly, the message demonstrates that the employee doesn’t consider these experiences to be an expected perk of employment. Instead, they recognize that someone made an effort to provide something of value.

When I don’t receive any acknowledgment after the event, I notice. While people sometimes forget or get busy, a consistent lack of expressed appreciation can create an impression of entitlement.  And entitlement is not a quality that encourages employers to invest in someone’s future career development.

Professional favors come in many forms. Your boss might invite you to sit at the company’s table at a major charity event, introduce you to an influential business contact or offer you an opportunity to attend an industry conference.

These gestures deserve more than casual acknowledgment.

Consider the invitation to a charity event. Your first responsibility is to RSVP promptly. RSVP comes from the French phrase Répondez, s’il vous plaît, meaning “Please respond.”

Yet responding to invitations isn’t something everyone does consistently. According to Greenvelope’s RSVP benchmarks, the response rate for conference and meeting invitations is approximately 66%.

Failing to respond promptly can make you appear disorganized or indifferent.

More importantly, recognize the invitation for what it represents: an opportunity to build professional relationships, demonstrate your interpersonal skills and potentially advance your career.

After attending, send a next-day thank-you message. Mention something specific you appreciated, such as an interesting conversation or a valuable introduction.

The same principle applies when a manager recommends you for a special assignment, provides career guidance or makes an introduction that expands your professional network.

Of course, you don’t need to write a formal note every time your boss buys you a cup of coffee. But meaningful favors deserve meaningful appreciation. When you thank someone immediately and follow up afterward, you have taken advantage of demonstrating gratitude twice.

Our SalesFuel research shows that 36% of B2B decision-makers will not do business with a sales professional who demonstrates poor etiquette. Even if you don’t work in sales, that finding should get your attention. Professional behavior influences how others perceive your credibility and character.

Some managers, particularly those from older generations, likely place considerable importance on traditional expressions of courtesy. Don’t miss these opportunities to show your character.

Job candidates typically have three major opportunities to impress prospective employers.

The first comes through their resumes, applications and assessment results. These materials help demonstrate whether candidates possess the skills and abilities required for the position.

The second opportunity occurs during the interview. Candidates can distinguish themselves by discussing their accomplishments, answering questions thoughtfully and communicating their career aspirations.

The third opportunity arrives after the interview ends. A well-written thank-you message sent within 24 hours can reinforce the positive impression you’ve worked hard to establish. This message shouldn’t be a generic, AI-generated paragraph that could be sent to any hiring manager.

Instead, reference something specific from your conversation. Perhaps you appreciated learning about the company’s growth plans or discussing a challenge the team hopes to solve. Briefly reaffirm your interest in the position and explain why the opportunity excites you.

In an age when AI can produce polished resumes and professional correspondence in seconds, genuine personalization matters more than ever. A thoughtful thank you demonstrates communication skills, attention to detail and an understanding of professional etiquette.

It also suggests something employers value: You recognize that another person invested time in considering your future.

A next-day thank-you doesn’t require elaborate language, expensive stationery or a lengthy message. Often, three or four sincere sentences are enough. What matters is the acknowledgment.

When someone gives you a gift, extends a favor or considers you for an opportunity, take the time to recognize their effort. You never know which professional relationship may influence your next promotion, assignment or career move.

Gratitude costs very little, but failing to express it can cost you opportunities. Make the next-day thank-you a habit that sets you apart.

The business world presents countless opportunities to make positive impressions that can influence your career trajectory. Whether you receive a thoughtful gift, benefit from a professional favor or interview for a new position, knowing when and how to express appreciation is an important professional skill.

Unfortunately, not everyone recognizes these moments for what they are: opportunities to demonstrate character, emotional intelligence and respect for others.

In my experience as a business owner, you can rarely go wrong by showing gratitude. A sincere thank-you email or text sent within 24 hours can distinguish you from colleagues and competitors who overlook this simple courtesy.

#5388. Andy Jassy’s prediction: Amazon could have two $1 trillion businesses within a decade

by Todd Bishop on Oct 29, 2026 at 6:08 pmOctober 31, 2026 at 8:51 am

No company has ever had a business with $1 trillion in annual revenue. Andy Jassy says Amazon is on a path to have two.

Amazon Web Services and the company’s stores business could both reach that milestone in the next five to 10 years, the Amazon CEO said Thursday in the company’s third-quarter earnings release and on its call with analysts.

It’s “pretty rare” for Jassy to make a projection that far out, Morgan Stanley analyst Brian Nowak observed on the call, asking how he gets there.

Jassy’s answer started with AWS, which is at a $184 billion annual revenue run rate after growing 39% in the third quarter. He expects growth of more than 40% in both 2027 and 2028, and pointed to a $578 billion backlog of contracted AWS revenue.

The largest customers reserve capacity in huge blocks, sometimes as much as a gigawatt at a time, giving Amazon “very good visibility” into 2027, 2028 and part of 2029, he said.

Beyond that, he said, businesses are still early in using AI, the cost of running AI models keeps falling, and new uses keep emerging, such as AI models finding and fixing security flaws.

“You can’t predict with any certainty five to 10 years from now, especially at these types of growth rates,” Jassy said of AWS. “But it’s not a stretch for us to imagine that this could be over a trillion dollar business.”

Jassy’s forecast is a big jump from seven months ago. In March, Jassy told employees that AWS had a chance to reach at least $600 billion in annual revenue within about a decade, double his earlier expectation, according to Reuters.

Amazon’s stores business is bigger than AWS. Sales from Amazon’s online and physical stores totaled $309 billion over the past 12 months, or about $575 billion if Jassy is including third-party seller services and advertising in his trillion-dollar projection. We’ve asked Amazon to clarify.

For comparison, Walmart, the world’s largest retailer, had $713 billion in revenue in its most recent fiscal year.

Whichever numbers he’s using, Jassy said “some folks are sleeping a bit” on how much progress the stores business has made.

Jassy argued that Amazon’s stores business is gaining ground on competitors. Amazon added more than $90 billion in gross sales over the past 12 months, he said, and is adding about twice as much per quarter as its next-largest U.S. competitor.

Units sold are up nearly 15% so far this year, Jassy said. He noted that nearly 80% of retail sales still happen in physical stores, which he expects to shift online over time.

The bold prediction came on a rough day for the company. Amazon shares fell more than 7% in after-hours trading after its profit fell short of Wall Street’s expectations.

It’s not going to be cheap to get there. Amazon expects to spend about $220 billion on capital projects this year, mostly for AWS, and Jassy said the company will spend “meaningfully more” in 2027. He said Amazon has “a clear line of sight to attractive financial returns” and is earning back its capital spending faster than before.

The impact is showing up in Amazon’s finances. Its free cash flow, the cash left over after capital spending, was negative $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with positive $14.8 billion a year earlier.

With its spending running ahead of the cash its businesses bring in, Amazon has raised $115 billion through long-term debt this year. Its interest expense more than tripled in the third quarter to $1.7 billion, cutting into its profit.

“We’re in the very early days of this inflection,” Jassy said. “Our strategy is working, and I expect it will for the foreseeable future.”

#5387. Coinbase CEO Predicts End of Subscription Era

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong is predicting that stablecoins and AI will reshape the way consumers pay for content on the internet, upending the subscription model that powers much of the web.

Armstrong posited this idea in an X post, where he claimed that stablecoins combined with the new x402 payment protocol will improve usability for businesses and consumers when it comes to micropayments for usage.

"Stablecoins and x402 enable businesses to accept micropayments for usage and decrease friction at checkout," the Coinbase CEO said.

Armstrong was particularly bullish on how x402 could disrupt online news subscriptions.

He argued that people shouldn't have to buy a monthly subscription just to read one article.

Instead, an AI agent could be tasked with retrieving the article on a consumer's behalf and would pay the publisher for that specific piece of content on autopilot.

The x402 technology powering Armstrong's vision is an open payment protocol that was first introduced by Coinbase in May 2025.

x402 is a reference to the HTTP 402 status code, meaning "Payment Required."

Although HTTP 402 has been around since the early days of the internet, it was never widely used for payments.

Coinbase's x402 protocol is designed to turn this largely dormant element of HTTP into an automated payment process that can facilitate transactions between websites, applications, and AI agents.

To illustrate, say you wanted an AI assistant to pull a certain article from a newspaper. Let's say it's priced at $0.25.

At this point, the AI agent can send a payment authorization for $0.25 in stablecoins, assuming the user has given the agent permission to make these payments.

Armstrong's views come as Coinbase and other big tech firms are pushing ahead with the infrastructure needed to facilitate AI payments.

In June, Coinbase teamed up with Amazon Web Services to enable publishers who use AWS CloudFront and Web Application Firewall to monetize the requests of AI agents through x402.

Separately, Cloudflare introduced its Monetization Gateway in closed beta in September. This allows participating businesses to request payments from AI agents for access to websites, datasets, and application programming interfaces through the x402 protocol.

#5386. A 30-Year-Old Ballerina-Turned-Billionaire Says to Avoid This Common Trap While Starting Your Own Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

She is the world’s youngest self-made female billionaire, unseating Taylor Swift and Lucy Guo.

As a teenager, Luana Lopes Lara studied ballet at the Bolshoi Theater School in Brazil. Competition was cutthroat; students sometimes tried to sabotage each other by hiding glass fragments in each other’s shoes. She attended technical school in the morning, then went to ballet training from the afternoon to the night.

“Since I was very little, I wanted to do big things,” Lopes Lara said in a recent episode of the podcast Confession with Ali Partovi.

That discipline laid the foundation for Lopes Lara’s later success. Now, at 30 years old, the entrepreneur is the world’s youngest self-made female billionaire, unseating pop star Taylor Swift and tech billionaire Lucy Guo in December 2025 to claim the title. Lopes Lara has a net worth of $2.6 billion, according to Forbes.

She made her fortune by co-founding Kalshi, a prediction market exchange where users can buy and sell yes-or-no contracts based on real-world future events, such as elections, economic data, weather and sports. Lopes Lara is working towards a future where people can essentially bet on anything.

Kalshi is “the first federally regulated exchange in the United States dedicated exclusively to trading on the outcomes of future events,” according to its site.

Lopes Lara said on the podcast that many smart founders fall into a common trap when it comes to starting their own business: They become “obsessed with probabilities.”

“You can psych yourself out of doing anything,” she said. “I think that going for it, taking the risk, believing that things will work out, is very important.”

Lopes Lara said that if a startup’s employees are only thinking about the math of whether the company is going to work or not, it becomes a “super negative culture that overreacts to every new information you have.”

“It’s important to have a lot of optimistic people who want to build things in the company,” Lopes Lara said.

Lopes Lara created Kalshi in 2018 with her co-founder, Tarek Mansour. They both graduated from the school in 2018. Lopes Lara majored in computer science and mathematics, while Mansour majored in electrical engineering, computer science and mathematics. They met because they had classes in common, and Lopes Lara always sat at the front of the class. Mansour wanted to learn from her example, so he started sitting next to her.

Lopes Lara came up with the idea for Kalshi when she was interning at Five Rings, a New York trading firm. She noticed that people on social media were pushing the narrative that reality TV star and entrepreneur Kylie Jenner was pregnant.

“I was like, ‘I want to make a bet with you on this,’” Lopes Lara said in an interview with Bloomberg earlier this year. The only problem was that she had nowhere to place the bet.

In that moment, Lopes Lara identified an opportunity that was bigger than gossip. She found that there were millions of people with firm views about the future, but no outlet for those beliefs.

Now Kalshi, which addresses that need, is worth a reported $22 billion and growing.

#5385. Power outage takes down KEXP streaming for Seattle radio station’s worldwide audience

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 2, 2026 at 8:22 am

KEXP’s website and online streaming were down Friday morning after a power outage hit the Seattle radio station, though its over-the-air broadcast was back and running.

The outage started around midnight, and the station was on and off for a while before it was “knocked offline by a major power outage” between 2 and 3 a.m., said Dashel Schueler, KEXP’s director of marketing and communications. Schueler didn’t know the cause of the outage.

The station’s backup power system, known as an uninterruptible power supply (UPS), also failed.

“There’s no power to the server room infrastructure because the UPS that is supposed to protect all of that gear has failed,” Schueler said. Staff are trying to power critical devices to restore services while they wait for the UPS to be repaired or for a workaround that bypasses it.

There’s no estimate yet for when streaming will return.

Listeners in the Seattle area can tune in at 90.3 FM. The outage affects the KEXP.org stream and the station’s mobile app. KEXP estimates about 175,000 people stream its live broadcast each week, and another 85,000 listen to its shows on-demand.

The outage also took down 92.7 KREV, the station KEXP now owns in the San Francisco Bay Area, which relies on KEXP’s Seattle-based digital infrastructure. Because KEXP’s DJs pick songs live rather than playing a preset playlist, underwriting breaks vary in timing and length, Schueler said. DJs fire the separate Seattle and Bay Area spots manually and at the same time.

KREV was back by around 8:30 to 8:45 a.m., running on a barebones setup KEXP typically uses for remote broadcasts, Schueler said. Listeners may notice some issues while the station gets everything put back together.

Around 7:30 a.m., KEXP DJ John Richards read messages on air from listeners across Seattle who were happy to have the station back — terrestrially at least.

A few posts from listeners on X and Bluesky referenced the streaming outage.

Update: Late Friday afternoon KEXP said it was still working to restore services, but it did manage to put up a temporary livestream on its site.

Update: KEXP CEO Ethan Raup details what went wrong and how it was fixed in this post on LinkedIn.

#5384. Solana Validator Admission Ticket: Who Fell Short After Alpenglow, and How Marinade Responded

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

StakeThat +MEV went into one of Solana's first Alpenglow epochs with about 137,000 SOL staked with it and 0.8169 SOL in its vote account. The new admission ticket required 0.8198 SOL. It was 0.003 SOL short.

That's the first post-activation picture of Solana's Validator Admission Ticket. Most stake made it through without trouble, but a small group of validators keeps dropping in and out, often by amounts smaller than a typical transaction fee. At least one large stake program changed its delegation code hours before activation so its stake wouldn't stay with those validators. Marinade's published validator snapshots for epochs 1063 to 1067 show who fell short and what happened next.

According to Solana's BLS Pubkey and VAT page, Alpenglow has been active on mainnet since epoch 1064, which began around 13:36 UTC on October 21. From then on, each validator's vote account pays a 0.8 SOL Validator Admission Ticket at the start of every epoch. The fee is burned, and it pays for the following epoch. The first charge, at the start of epoch 1064, covered epoch 1065.

The rules are strict. If the fee can't be paid, Solana's page says, "your validator does not vote or produce blocks in the next epoch." Validators without a registered BLS key, or outside the top 2,000 by stake, are also excluded. Delegators to an excluded validator earn no inflation rewards for that epoch. The page also stresses that the balance "has to stay funded, not be funded once."

The vote account also has to stay above its rent-exempt minimum. In Marinade's data, the full requirement works out to 0.8197612 SOL.

Marinade publishes the inputs to its stake auction every epoch in a public pipeline repository. The input data checks whether each validator's vote account holds enough to cover the next epoch's ticket. Each snapshot covers about 670 validators and roughly 438 million SOL of stake.

Before activation, in the epoch 1063 snapshot, 33 validators holding 7.63 million SOL, or 1.74% of stake, were below the ticket balance. Once Alpenglow went live, that number fell quickly: 15 validators with 1.55 million SOL (0.35%) in epoch 1064, then 19 with 1.15 million (0.26%) in epoch 1065, the first epoch the ticket actually paid for. By epoch 1066 it was 13 validators with 790,000 SOL (0.18%), and by epoch 1067 just 8 with 710,000 SOL (0.16%).

The epoch 1063 count matches a figure in Marinade's own code history. A commit on October 21 notes that its new gate "refuses the 33 validators with vat_eligible false" in the 1063 snapshot.

The biggest pre-activation gaps were fixed in time. An unnamed validator with 2.05 million SOL of stake, Temporal Emerald with 1.23 million and Bitget Wallet with 593,000 were all below the ticket balance in epoch 1063. All three had topped up by the next snapshot. Of the 33 flagged before activation, 25 had recovered by epoch 1064.

So the fee didn't remove a large share of stake. The balance check affected less than 2% of stake at its peak, and about 0.16% by epoch 1067.

The validators that did fall short show a pattern: many of them nearly had enough.

Because the ticket is charged every epoch, a validator that tops up just enough to pass once will fail again an epoch later unless it adds more. Between epochs 1064 and 1067, between 3 and 11 validators fell below the threshold each epoch, while a similar number recovered.

The shortfalls also cut across setups. Every validator flagged in epoch 1067 runs either Agave 4.3.x, the client release the migration required, or the latest Firedancer build. Software readiness wasn't the issue. Keeping the balance funded was.

Solana offers a fix: routing block revenue to the vote account through solana vote-update-commission-collector. That keeps the account funded automatically, though the change takes two epochs to apply.

The bigger story is how stake programs reacted. Marinade, one of Solana's largest delegation programs, changed its auction code in pull request #153, merged at about 06:47 UTC on October 21, roughly seven hours before Alpenglow activated.

The change adds a new disqualifying condition, vatIneligible. A validator whose vat_eligible flag is false "gets no SAM and no backstop stake," because "Agave then pays its stakers no inflation rewards for the epoch." A null value never disqualifies a validator. The check currently tests only the SIMD-0357 balance, not BLS key registration.

The first version applied the rule only in Alpenglow epochs. Marinade's developers then caught a timing problem. Agave starts charging the ticket at the 1063-to-1064 boundary, and "a stake move made in epoch E takes effect in E+1," so the original rule "left Marinade stake on refused validators for epochs 1064 and 1065." The merged version refuses ineligible validators in every epoch.

The snapshots confirm it worked. In the epoch 1064 snapshot, 192,762 SOL of Marinade stake sat on ineligible validators, nearly all of it on one unnamed validator. By epoch 1065, that had dropped to 2,407 SOL, and by epoch 1066 to 10 SOL. A later commit gives the rule its own label and call to action in Marinade's interface, so operators can see why they've been excluded.

Marinade, in short, turned a protocol fee into a delegation rule of its own. A validator that misses one ticket loses an epoch of rewards, and it also loses Marinade stake until its balance recovers.

Before activation, Solana Compass reported that a community tracker flagged 45% of stake as not ready two days ahead of epoch 1064, mostly validators on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1. The following day, that had dropped to 20.3%.

Marinade's snapshots show the software gap closing much as those warnings suggested it needed to. Stake on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1 fell from 6.56% in epoch 1063 to 0.08% by epoch 1067. Firedancer operators, who had to switch to Agave for the migration, dropped from 11.0% of stake to 5.9% in epoch 1064. They then came back strongly, reaching 17.2% by epoch 1067, well above their pre-migration share.

The large readiness gap was about software and keys, and it was mostly closed by the time it mattered. The fee gap was always small.

For most delegators, nothing changed: more than 99.8% of stake sits with validators that keep their tickets paid. For those delegated to the few that don't, the cost is clear: no inflation rewards for that epoch, and in Marinade's case, stake moved elsewhere.

The protocol sets one requirement: 0.8 SOL in the vote account every epoch. Stake programs are now adding their own rules on top, starting with Marinade's. Validators that keep running near the threshold will keep losing epochs of rewards, and possibly delegations, until they keep a buffer or automate funding.

#5382. Metal fabricator NIC Global to cut 103 jobs near Seattle, move production to Eastern Washington

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 30, 2026 at 10:24 amOctober 30, 2026 at 10:25 am

Metal fabricator NIC Global plans to close its Woodinville, Wash., plant, eliminating 103 jobs. Declining business from local customers is prompting the company to shift production primarily to Eastern Washington to meet data center-related growth.

The layoffs are scheduled to begin Jan. 18, 2027, with final departures Aug. 31, 2028, according to a notice filed with the Washington Employment Security Department. Affected jobs include assembly, engineering, quality assurance, metal fabrication specialists, and forklift positions.

The building will be returned to its landlord when the lease ends in September 2028.

“This is a sad day for our company. Woodinville is where NIC was formed — three Seattle-area sheet-metal shops brought together under one roof in 2001 — and the people in that building built the foundation of everything NIC is today,” Troy Wood, company president and CEO, said via email.

The 100,000-square-foot site mostly served energy and medical device customers. Wood said the volume of work at the plant has declined while demand has increased in Eastern Washington for customers building power distribution technology needed by data centers.

“NIC is a supplier of sheet-metal fabrications and assemblies, and in our business, being close to our customers is what keeps us competitive,” Wood said.

While most of the work from Woodinville will go to Spokane, and a smaller portion will go to NIC’s Gallatin, Tenn., facility. The company also has manufacturing in Pullman; Chillicothe, Ohio; and Denton, Texas. The work outside of Washington is focused on the heavy truck sector. The company’s headcount is nearly 600.

Laid-off workers will be encouraged to apply for openings at other plants.

There are smaller fabricators remaining in the Seattle area, including JEMCO Components & Fabrications, which provides precision machining and sheet-metal fabrication for customers in medical, aerospace and defense sectors, and QUAL-FAB serving medical and dental customers.

NIC’s legal and financial headquarters will stay in the Woodinville area, where the company plans a new office for its finance, IT, sales and West Coast support teams.

Wood praised the quality and reliability of the Woodinville employees’ work.

“I am grateful to every one of them,” he said, “and especially to those who chose to stay with us through two and a half years of uncertainty and kept doing their jobs with integrity.”

Decentralized platform Hyperliquid has permanently removed 49.87 million native HYPE tokens from circulation, which amounts to almost 5% of its maximum supply of 1 billion units. On-chain monitoring confirms that the combined fiat value of the destroyed assets has reached $3.89 billion at the current market rate.

The supply reduction happens automatically: the protocol converts fee revenue into continuous token buybacks from the open market as the platform's historical revenue has surpassed the $1.38 billion mark.

The mechanism relies on the Assistance Fund, a system smart contract without private keys, whose balance was officially recognized as burned in December 2025 by a decision of 85% of the network's validators. Between 97% and 99% of the exchange's trading fees are directed here.

Over the past 24 hours, this engine destroyed 19,700 HYPE (about $1.59 million) against daily protocol fees of $1.69 million. Of the platform's $1.38 billion in total revenue, $63.52 million was generated over the past 30 days.

In addition to standard trading fees, Hyperliquid's architecture uses additional automated deflation channels:

Since the buyback is strictly denominated in US dollars, the exact rate of token destruction fluctuates depending on the market. At current asset prices of around $78–$80, the net volume of tokens withdrawn per dollar of fees decreases.

The ecosystem's long-term deflationary status now directly depends on whether fee generation can consistently outpace the scheduled vesting for the team and early contributors, which adds about 9.9 million HYPE tokens to circulation every month.

At the current pace of 19,700 tokens per day, buybacks would absorb roughly 591,000 HYPE per month, offsetting only about 6% of these unlocks, which means net circulating supply is still expanding despite the burn.
