Ripple's Swell event kicked off with a bang on October 28, 2026, bringing together decision-makers from traditional finance, crypto, academia and the XRP ecosystem.

In one session highlighted by the official Swell X account, Johann Kerbrat, Senior VP and GM of Crypto at Robinhood, joined Ripple President Monica Long to discuss the evolution of crypto markets, expanding access to digital assets and the future of global financial services.

Tokenization took the main stage at The Shed 🌊 Robinhood's @JohannKerbrat sat down with Ripple President @MonicaLongSF to talk tokenization, crypto markets and what's next for @RobinhoodApp. https://t.co/I7X2E2MMxl

As Robinhood pushes into always-on markets through blockchain technology, the two crypto executives discussed the "unstoppable freight train" of tokenization and what was needed to build the future of global financial services on-chain.

Tokenization involves representing real-world or traditional financial assets as digital tokens on a blockchain, and it is attracting growing attention because it could enable assets to be issued, transferred, and managed through blockchain-based infrastructure.

Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse shares this same viewpoint, saying that as traditional and digital finance converge, market infrastructure is migrating to modern rails. Settlement is moving to real-time, 24/7 and tokenized assets can be traded, financed and used as collateral.

Robinhood will integrate Ripple Treasury to modernize and automate its global treasury operations, including cash and liquidity management, cash flow forecasting, payments, risk management, and intercompany netting. The financial services provider will leverage RLUSD on the XRPL for institutional settlement, extending the stablecoin's utility across Bitstamp by Robinhood's growing institutional business.

#5379. Filing: Chip startup Powerlattice raises $86M to ease AI’s power crunch

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 30, 2026 at 11:30 amOctober 30, 2026 at 3:35 pm

Powerlattice, a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.

The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.

AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.

“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou, Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.; San Jose, Calif.; and Hsinchu, Taiwan.

Earlier this week, Powerlattice announced it had demonstrated what it calls the industry’s first monolithic integrated voltage regulator chiplet, which packs the controller, power transistors and inductors onto a single piece of silicon.

In the test, the chiplet powered a device Powerlattice built to mimic the fast-shifting electrical loads of next-generation AI accelerators. The company says multiple chiplets can be linked to work as one, letting chip designers match the setup to their processors.

“Breaking through the AI power wall requires us to rethink how power reaches the processor,” Zou said in the announcement.

#5378. My Layoff Was a Blessing in Disguise. The Business I Started on Instagram Is on Track for $168,000 This Year.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Abigail Morris followed her life-long passion into business.

This as-told-to story is based on a conversation with Abigail Morris, founder of Chicago-based full-service interior design studio Abigail Morris Interiors. In 2022, Morris started her interior design business on the side, building it as she continued her full-time career in corporate tech. After being laid off at the end of 2024, Morris went all-in on her business. The piece has been edited for length and clarity.

I’ve been doing interior design in some form or other my entire life without really realizing it. Mostly in giving unsolicited advice growing up — I always had strong opinions on colors and fabrics and things like that. But it wasn’t until much later that I realized I could pursue it as a career, which sounds silly. My family, with the best of intentions, encouraged me to go to business school and start a career that felt safe. So I worked in corporate tech for about 10 years.

Then, like many people during the pandemic, I had time to reevaluate. Am I really happy with what I’m doing? What’s next for me? I decided to follow that original passion for design. It felt like a now or never moment. So I took interior design classes at The Art Institute of Chicago. I got a certificate there, then started an interior design Instagram. I wanted people to know I was open for business. But I continued working full-time in corporate tech because I was still a little afraid to go all-in. I had a very comfortable job; I had the golden handcuffs.

Then, near the end of 2024, I got laid off. It was such a blessing in disguise — the universe setting me free to go all-in on my business. It was around that point that I also shifted focus to restoring historic residential and commercial properties. I have such a reverence and a passion for historic homes. They were just made with so much more attention to detail and craftsmanship.

My husband and I moved into our 1889 row home here in Chicago. Before I was laid off, I did a bunch of updates to our home and had it photographed. That helped me add to my portfolio on Instagram. The first few clients that reached out to me had also had historic homes and were attracted to me because I had that in my portfolio. The business snowballed from there. I get a lot of requests to work on historic homes here in the city and have started fielding some requests from further out in the Midwest and even on the West Coast. In the past couple months, I’ve gotten more requests for people who have newer builds who want that feeling of a more historic, character-rich home.

Earlier this year, I worked on the St. Elmo Hotel in Ouray, Colorado. I was connected with the owner, who also has a passion for preserving historic buildings. So he and his hospitality group had already done one project in Montrose, Colorado and were looking for a designer to work on a building that had a lot of original features. The goal was to celebrate those characteristics but also bring the design into the 21st century with more modern comforts. Because I already had experience working on a hotel on the National Register of Historic Places, they pulled me in.

Designing for historic properties requires discipline. A lot of times, when you go into a space and you’re redesigning, you’re starting from scratch and reimagining everything. But that’s not the case with historic properties. We have to think about what we can preserve. For example, in the St. Elmo Hotel, we kept as much wallpaper on the walls as we could. We didn’t remove any of the wainscoting or things like that and did a lot of repairs to bring things back to their original glory. So it’s about having an eye for editing before making any big design decisions.

During the first year in business, I was still getting my sea legs. I was still working full-time; it was really trial by fire. So my take-home pay was around $48,000 the first year. And I reinvested into the business significantly. Project photography is always a big investment. I also worked with a stylist and videographer. This past year, I’m on track for about $168,000 for the year. And my take-home pay will probably be around $100,000. The rest I’ll reinvest into the business — PR, project photography, etc. I’ve also brought on someone to help me edit social media reels because that’s a full time job in and of itself.

Next, I plan to make some more strategic hires to help me scale. Right now, I’m wearing too many hats. I don’t have enough time to do the design work and scale the business and client experience the way I want to. I do have a CPA and a bookkeeper, and I had an intern over the summer. But it would be great to have more support for procurement, technical drawings and other assistant tasks. I’m actually actively interviewing people this week.

In addition to hiring and scaling the business, one of the biggest challenges and opportunities ahead is the impact of AI. Currently, I use Claude and ChatGPT to help with some back-office tasks, like organizing the notes I take on my iPad while on a job site. But I’m seeing a lot of clients come in with designs they’ve made with AI, asking how to translate that to their rooms. On one hand, that’s great — I want people to have access to these tools. But these tools also require education. People have to understand that just because AI generates this picture, that doesn’t mean it’s structurally possible to implement. Or maybe it includes a specific chair that doesn’t exist.

In our current era, with AI and technology moving at the speed of light, I think people are really going to start to value craftsmanship. I think we’re going to have an arts and crafts renaissance. And I’m looking forward to how that plays out. The original arts and crafts revival in the U.S. was a result of the Industrial Revolution. Everybody was like, “We’re tired of having all this mass-produced, not well-made stuff.” We’re absolutely seeing that now. People crave a little bit of that imperfection in their home. They gravitate toward items that look like somebody actually made them with their hands versus in a machine across the ocean.

The world is getting wilder and wilder, and people definitely want to have respite in their home. They want that layered, cozy vibe. I’m really excited to be part of that.

#5377. Madrona Prize goes to UW research on agents that shrink AI models to run on small chips

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 3:13 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 11:53 am

A University of Washington project that uses AI agents to squeeze AI models onto tiny devices — such as a solar-powered camera that spots elk in the wild — won the Madrona Prize at the Allen School’s annual Research Showcase on Thursday.

Seattle venture capital firm Madrona has awarded the prize since 2006 to Allen School student projects that combine strong research with commercial potential. The winners were chosen from among the student posters presented at the evening event on the UW campus.

Zhihan Zhang, a PhD student in the Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, presented the winning project. It tests whether AI agents can do a job that experts now do by hand: shrinking AI models and tuning device software to run on small, low-power chips with tight limits on memory, power and heat.

In the team’s tests, leading AI models failed at the task without feedback from real hardware. The team built a system that let the agent load its work onto real hardware, measure the results and try again. With that feedback, the agent beat human experts within seven rounds.

The researchers used the approach on two real-world projects: an elk-detection camera trap, which needed its vision model shrunk by 250 times, and a wearable device that records children’s speech for child development research.

The team released its benchmark, called Embedded Arena, as open-source code. Allen School faculty members Shwetak Patel, Vikram Iyer, Natasha Jaques and Kurtis Heimerl also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Alexander Metzger, Jiuyang Lyu, Chun-Cheng Chang, Jiayi Shao, Yujia Liu, Emmanuel Azuh Mensah, Edward Wang and Gregory D. Abowd.

The People’s Choice award went to Keisuke Kamahori for VibeSys, a project that uses AI agents to write custom software for a specific chip and task, then keep improving it, instead of relying on general-purpose tools built for common setups.

Its first application, VibeServe, writes the behind-the-scenes software that takes requests from users and runs them through an AI model. On Amazon’s Trainium2 chips, the software it built handled up to 2.7 times as much work as an existing system. Shihang (Vic) Li and Allen School faculty members Simon Peter and Baris Kasikci also worked on the project.

The first runner-up for the Madrona Prize, Tanush Yadav, presented VideoNet, a test of how well AI models recognize specific actions in video, such as a particular bouldering move or a type of surgical stitch. It covers more than 1,000 actions across 38 fields.

Leading AI models struggle with it compared to ordinary people. Shown three examples, people improved their accuracy by about 14 percentage points, while AI models improved by about 3 percentage points.

Allen School faculty members Ali Farhadi, Hanna Hajishirzi and Ranjay Krishna, and former Allen School faculty member Yejin Choi, now at Stanford University, also worked on the project.

Other collaborators: Mohammadreza Salehi, Jae Sung Park, Vivek Ramanujan and Rohun Tripathi.

The second runner-up, Henry Wong, presented work on securing benchtop DNA synthesizers, machines that let users print synthetic DNA.

His project focuses on protecting the screening software meant to stop someone from printing a dangerous pathogen, and concludes that even perfectly secure hardware wouldn’t fully solve the problem.

Allen School faculty member Jeff Nivala and former Allen School faculty member Tadayoshi Kohno, now at Georgetown University, also worked on the project.

All of the presenters are PhD students in the Allen School.

Correction: An earlier version of this story misidentified Sethu Raman of Madrona in the lead photo caption.

#5376. XRP Ledger Hits Highest Level of 2026

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

XRP Ledger activity has jumped to its highest level this year, while the price of XRP slips lower. Active accounts, which count the unique senders on the network, reached 32,604 on October 27. That is the highest reading since the start of 2026 and well above the 30-day average of 19.4K.

For most of the past year, daily active accounts stayed between 13K and 20K. A few short spikes pushed above 30K, but they faded quickly. The latest jump is larger and cleaner than those moves. It also follows a deep drop in late August and early September, when activity fell to nearly 4K accounts.

The numbers have cooled since the peak. The latest reading is 30.5K, down 6.3% in 24 hours, and the chart shows a sharp pullback toward 18K. Even so, the network is far busier than it was a few weeks ago. The all-time high of 106K is still far away, so the ledger has a long way to go before it reaches record levels.

The price chart does not match the surge in usage. XRP trades near $1.29 and has been falling since early October, when it was close to $1.50. The coin is now below the 50-day and 100-day averages, which sit around $1.33 and $1.36. The 200-day average near $1.37 is also above the price. All of these now act as resistance.

Support is near $1.25, where buyers stepped in twice in recent weeks. If that level breaks, the next area to watch is $1.20, followed by the August breakout area near $1.10 to $1.15. Volume has stayed low throughout the decline, and the RSI sits just below 50. This indicates the market is neutral and lacks strong momentum in either direction.

A rise in active accounts can mean more people are using the network for payments, trading, or moving funds. That is a healthy signal for the long term. But network activity does not always push the price up in the short term. Spikes can also come from bots, airdrops, or one-time events, and they often fade quickly, as past peaks this year have shown.

For XRP to turn bullish, the price needs to climb back above $1.33 and then $1.37. Until that happens, the trend remains weak, and the busy ledger stays a positive sign that the market has not yet rewarded.

#5375. I Took Back My Team’s Decisions During a Crisis — and Forgot to Give Them Back. Here’s How to Delegate Responsibly.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Pressure makes owners reclaim every hard call. Without an exit condition, that temporary grip becomes how the company decides.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

The week a key hire quit mid-project, I took three routine calls back onto my desk “just until we stabilize.” Pricing exceptions. Vendor swaps. The weekly staffing puzzle. The crunch lasted about ten days. The habit lasted months.

I remember the quiet after more than the scramble. People stopped bringing recommendations. They brought questions. I had taught them, without meaning to, that judgment lived upstairs again.

Here’s my situation, so you know where I’m coming from. I run B:Side Capital, a mission-driven Small Business Administration (SBA) lender and certified community development financial institution (CDFI). I also teach management and entrepreneurship at Arizona State University’s W.P. Carey School of Business. Across those chairs I keep seeing the same pattern in restaurants, contractors, clinics and software shops: When pressure arrives, the owner becomes the decision system, and nobody writes the date when that arrangement ends.

Most owners treat a temporary grab of authority as common sense. It often is. Speed matters when consequences are coupled and information is thin. The failure is leaving the grab unnamed. Temporary control becomes institutional culture unless you define the evidence for returning decisions to their normal owners. Gallup finds that employees whose manager involved them in setting goals were nearly four times more likely to be engaged than others, yet only 30% of employees experience that basic expectation. Involvement dies first when every hard call routes back to one desk.

I used to treat the pull-up as proof I was carrying the load. Wrong lesson. Carrying the load can be necessary. Teaching the company that only you may decide is optional and expensive.

Start with a blank page and the decisions that repeat every week. Pricing exceptions. Hiring offers inside a band. Vendor changes under a dollar threshold. Schedule swaps. Customer make-goods. Write who may decide, what they may trade and when the call must move up. Goals without owners are theater. Strategy becomes real the moment someone knows, without asking, whether the call is theirs.

At BodeTree, I finally did this after another stretch where every exception landed in my inbox. The map was ugly in its simplicity. Ambition had concentrated judgment in one person, and I had been calling that leadership.

The principle fits in one line: Decision rights are part of strategy, not an org-chart afterthought.

Try the same map this week. Pick five recurring calls. Put a name next to each. If your name appears four times, you have a concentration, whether you plan to grow or not. A restaurant owner might find the same person owns menu specials, vendor credits and the Saturday floor. A SaaS founder might find discounting, enterprise renewals and production access share one login. Name the owners while the room is still listening.

Delegation is incomplete until the person receiving authority knows when and how to return a decision upward. Local actors need room to act, and they also hit threshold changes the original mandate did not anticipate. An escalation path defines the triggers, the response time and what context must travel with the issue. Skip it, and you get silent overreach or habitual upward deferral. Both train the wrong muscle.

I fought writing triggers because they felt bureaucratic. They are a boundary, not a binder. Act here. Come back when one of these conditions changes: risk crosses the band, purpose conflicts, spend exceeds the limit or two teams need the same scarce resource.

The principle: Hand someone the return path with the authority.

Say the split plainly when you delegate. “You own this up to X. Escalate when Y. Bring the context, not just the question.” A franchisee can do that for a regional manager. A clinic owner can do it for billing leads. A fabricator can do it for shift supervisors. Keep one annoyance unresolved on purpose: the issue that always climbs because nobody knows whether it belongs downstairs. That gap is the curriculum.

Crisis can justify concentrating authority. Comfort cannot. The moment you pull a decision upward, state what would let it move back down: a date, a restored capability, a risk threshold or an information flow that no longer needs your desk. Review observed capability against decisions people actually got to practice. Otherwise the exit test measures deprivation of opportunity as if it were incapacity.

I used to wait until things “felt normal” before returning calls. Feelings are a weak criterion. Normal never arrives cleanly. The temporary grip stays because returning authority requires a second act of courage: trusting judgment you recently starved.

The principle: A pull-up without an exit condition is a theory of leadership in disguise.

Test it this week. List every decision you reclaimed in the last quarter “just until we stabilize.” Write one sentence for each: what would justify giving it back, and who must explain if it stays with you. A retailer can stage a seasonal buy back to a buyer. A professional-services owner can return staffing puzzles to a lead. Ambition stays. The calendar gets a veto on permanent centralization.

Here’s where I’d start this week: Map five recurring calls to named owners, write escalation triggers beside each one and put a dated exit condition on every temporary pull-up still sitting on your desk. Say the return path out loud to whoever shares the risk with you.

The quiet after that quit still sits in my mind. People waiting for my nod was the real scoreboard. Write the exit condition when you take the call back, and judgment has somewhere to live again.

The week a key hire quit mid-project, I took three routine calls back onto my desk “just until we stabilize.” Pricing exceptions. Vendor swaps. The weekly staffing puzzle. The crunch lasted about ten days. The habit lasted months.

I remember the quiet after more than the scramble. People stopped bringing recommendations. They brought questions. I had taught them, without meaning to, that judgment lived upstairs again.

I run B:Side Capital, a mission-driven Small Business Administration (SBA) lender and certified community development financial institution (CDFI). I also teach management and entrepreneurship at Arizona State University’s W.P. Carey School of Business. Across those chairs I keep seeing the same pattern in restaurants, contractors, clinics and software shops: When pressure arrives, the owner becomes the decision system, and nobody writes the date when that arrangement ends.

#5374. Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 5:21 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 6:29 am

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer, an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday, saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.

In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.

“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.

“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.

He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.

Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.

Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.

“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”

The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it stripped the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records, including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to the group, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive.

A press representative for the group sent a statement from Nick Streuli, an officer of Washington Needs to Compete. Streuli runs the government relations firm Sundial Advocacy and was previously policy and outreach director for former Gov. Jay Inslee.

“Washington Needs to Compete is committed to our state and wants to see it succeed,” Streuli said in the statement. “Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to invest and grow here. We are starting a conversation about our economic challenges and how to solve them.”

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”

It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.

The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.

In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall, up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.

Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website, Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.

The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.

The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

Updated Nov. 2 with comment from Washington Needs to Compete.

#5372. ‘Google Slides and PowerPoint Are Dead.’ Did AI Really Kill the Corporate Deck?

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Another casualty of AI might be the PowerPoint and Google Slide presentation. Many are now using coding to create decks.

PowerPoint may soon be facing match point. People have been predicting the death of presentation software for decades, but AI strategist Peter Gostev reignited the debate last week with a LinkedIn post declaring “Google Slides & PowerPoint are dead,” according to LinkedIn News.

Why? The argument is that AI can now build interactive, web-based presentations from a simple prompt. Anthropic’s Claude Design turns a rough outline into an on-brand deck that exports as standalone HTML, as well as PowerPoint. Microsoft is fighting back by building AI editing directly into PowerPoint, and says new-user retention for the feature jumped 36%.

But some business owners are hungry for a new way to communicate. AI coach Braydon Carter says entrepreneurs at a recent mastermind asked him to teach them how he builds his presentations as websites using AI coding tools.

Not everyone is a fan. Skeptics point out that HTML decks are hard to edit without AI, and some corporate email filters block HTML attachments. E-Tabs founder Benjamin Rietti doesn’t think PowerPoint is going anywhere. What’s dying, he says, is “the old way of producing those decks”: the late nights, endless copying and pasting, and last-minute number checks.

#5367. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

#5366. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

#5364. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

#5363. Crypto and Midterm Election: 3 Risks From Trump’s $5,000 Stimulus to Iran

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Crypto is facing a major political test as Americans head to the polls on November 3, with the US midterm election potentially reshaping regulation, stimulus expectations, and investor risk appetite.

Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress, while Democrats are seeking to regain power in at least one chamber. The outcome could determine if President Donald Trump advances his economic agenda or faces a tougher legislative road ahead.

For crypto, the midterm election comes with three major risks: Trump’s proposed $5,000 stimulus dividend, the future of stalled crypto legislation, and escalating tensions with Iran.

The election itself may not immediately change Crypto’s fundamentals. However, it could shift expectations around liquidity, regulation, and the financial markets.

Trump has promised a $5,000 dividend payment to adult US citizens if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate. The proposal would cover 240 million adults, potentially costing around $1.2 trillion, and Trump has also suggested that tariff revenue could help fund the payments.

Trump may have just sealed the deal on stage in Dallas.He's promising a $5,000 dividend to every American adult if Republicans win the midterms — only condition is the money has to be spent in the U.S.I've never seen anything like this. pic.twitter.com/ypJP2fYsLj

A Republican victory could then strengthen expectations for additional household spending and potentially inject fresh liquidity into financial markets. We, in the crypto market, have historical reasons to watch stimulus closely.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, US stimulus checks coincided with extraordinary monetary easing and a powerful crypto rally. A Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland study found that the 2020 payments increased Bitcoin buy volume by 3.8%, while the associated price effect was modest.

The 2020–2021 rally also benefited from low interest rates, institutional adoption, and abundant liquidity. Hence, a new stimulus program could encourage retail investors to allocate more money toward Bitcoin and other risk assets.

However, the proposed dividend is not approved, and higher inflation expectations or Treasury yields could offset some of the bullish impact. If Democrats win control of Congress, Trump’s proposal could face a much tougher path toward approval.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The Midterm election could also determine whether lawmakers make progress on the most-awaited crypto regulation, the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act. It aims to establish clearer rules governing digital assets and the division of responsibilities between US regulators.

The bill remains stalled after failing to advance through a Senate procedural vote in September. A Republican victory could improve its chances, although bipartisan support would still be necessary to overcome legislative hurdles.

A Democratic victory, particularly if the party takes control of the House, could bring increased scrutiny of Trump’s crypto-related ventures and campaign connections. That could delay legislation as lawmakers focus on investigations and oversight.

Still, a Democratic win would not automatically mean tougher crypto regulation. Bipartisan support for clearer digital asset rules remains possible, although the final legislation could look different from the current proposal.

The Midterm election presents a mixed outlook for crypto. A Republican victory combined with stimulus optimism, progress on crypto legislation, and Iran de-escalation would create a potentially bullish environment.

A Democratic victory could introduce regulatory uncertainty, while renewed conflict in the Middle East could pressure crypto regardless of the midterm election result. For us, the key question is whether political optimism can outweigh geopolitical risk.

Trump’s stimulus promise may offer a powerful bullish narrative, but crypto’s next major move could ultimately depend on improving liquidity or another inflationary shock.

The biggest immediate threat to crypto is not the midterm election, and it may come from outside Washington. The US carried out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm islands near the Strait of Hormuz. This revived concerns about escalation, even as diplomatic contacts continued.

Long liquidations occur when traders betting on higher prices are forced to close their positions, typically after losses push their margin balances below required levels. When large numbers of leveraged positions are liquidated in a short period, the resulting selling can intensify downward price pressure.

Along these lines, Dogecoin was down nearly 3% in the last 24 hours to $0.078 as the market fell while investors digested the Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady at its October meeting.

Dogecoin rose for three consecutive days earlier in the week to hit $0.08, but profit-taking in the markets caused its price to retreat.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures Index—the Fed's preferred inflation gauge—was released Thursday, with few cryptocurrencies recouping losses in the wake of the report.

The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6% as the pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target.

While the Fed held interest rates on Wednesday, as expected, two officials dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase and Chair Kevin Warsh declined to signal what might come in December. However, expectations for a 25 basis point hike at the central bank's next meeting on Dec. 9 remain.

#5361. Who gets your vote? What rumors should you spot? Election quiz and bingo offer guidance

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 2, 2026 at 10:28 am

With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault, a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat, a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.

“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.

The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.

Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.

“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.

Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post. “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud. Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”

#5359. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.

#5357. Accent bias: AI models penalize certain speakers in interviews and tests, UW study finds

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 2:50 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 2:50 pm

Picture two job candidates giving the same answer to the same interview question, word for word. One has an American accent. The other has a Nigerian accent. Ask a leading AI model to score them, and the American will likely come out ahead.

That’s the gist of new research from the University of Washington, which tested how AI models from Google, OpenAI and Alibaba evaluated English spoken with five accents: American, British, Chinese, Indian and Nigerian.

Across job interviews, conference presentations and English proficiency tests, the models generally ranked American and British speakers highest, Indian speakers in the middle, and Chinese and Nigerian speakers lowest.

The penalty fell mostly on delivery. But content scores for Chinese and Nigerian speakers sometimes slipped, too, even though every speaker read the same script and the models were told to judge only the substance.

“Even though they repeatedly claimed Chinese and Nigerian speakers ‘mumbled’ or were ‘difficult to understand,’ the models were actually very good at transcribing the accented speech,” said Orevaoghene Ahia, a UW doctoral student in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering and co-lead author of the study.

The stakes go beyond a bad review. Companies increasingly use AI to screen recorded job interviews, and instructors are turning to oral exams as written work gets easier to fake with AI. At least one major English test used for visas and immigration, Pearson’s PTE Academic, relies on AI to score some spoken answers. It was given about 1.2 million times in 2023, according to figures cited in the paper.

The researchers didn’t test the actual products used by hiring platforms or test makers. How those systems work is usually not public, and the paper notes there are no public audits of AI-scored English tests that the authors know of. Instead, the team tested general-purpose models that companies could build on.

“We wanted to check these state-of-the-art models because these are what companies would deploy in a real-world setting,” said Yulia Tsvetkov, a UW associate professor in the Allen School and the study’s senior author.

The research was funded in part by gifts from Google and OpenAI, whose models were among those tested.

To understand the pattern, the researchers measured how acoustically different each accent was from American English. Chinese and Nigerian accents were the farthest away, and models’ scores dropped as that distance grew. Indian and British accents sat close to the American baseline.

The researchers suggest the bias may come from training data that describes accented speakers as unclear, from data sets that underrepresent some accents, or from training that reinforces ideas about how a professional should sound. English is an official language in Nigeria and the language of instruction in Indian schools, yet both accents scored below American and British ones.

The study is the latest in a run of UW research on AI bias. Earlier projects found that AI models favored resumes with white- and male-associated names, that politically slanted chatbots could shift people’s views, and that AI-written children’s stories nearly erased female animal characters.

The team presented the research Oct. 25 at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing in Budapest. Next, the researchers plan to study more accents, including regional variations within countries, and to look at how AI models handle audio in medical settings such as automated emergency response.

“For all of these, we hope that developers build and publish evaluations of their models that don’t focus only on average performance, but also break it down into subpopulations, dialects and so on,” Tsvetkov said. “We don’t want the average performance to be 97% accurate for the general population, but for a smaller group only 20%.”

#5356. Gemini Boss Slams Crypto-Hater Lagarde Following Her Resignation Announcement

Gemini co-founder Tyler Winklevoss took a jab at European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde after her unexpected resignation announcement.

"Your legacy will be to fight crypto and fail. Good luck in your next endeavor!" Winklevoss commented on Lagarde's resignation announcement on X.

Lagarde announced today that she will resign from her position on Feb. 7, 2027, which will be about nine months before her eight-year term is supposed to be over.

The ECB president, who has been at the helm of the ECB since November 2019, thanked her colleagues and those who have supported her over the past seven years.

It has been confirmed that the selection of her successor will be carried out by the European Council.

Lagarde has long been an outspoken critic of cryptocurrencies, especially Bitcoin.

Back in January 2021, she characterized Bitcoin as a very speculative asset. She also accused the cryptocurrency of enabling illicit financial operations.

During the Reuters Next conference, Lagarde said Bitcoin has been used for "funny business" and money laundering. Lagarde called for global coordination of regulations on cryptocurrencies.

The criticism further escalated when Lagarde said in May 2022 that cryptocurrencies are worth virtually nothing.

"My very humble assessment is that it is worth nothing," Lagarde said during an interview on Dutch television.

Lagarde stated that cryptocurrencies do not have underlying assets that would give investors a solid anchor of safety.

She also warned about inexperienced retail investors risking their savings in speculative crypto investments.

The ECB president also shared that one of her sons had made investments in cryptocurrencies despite her warnings.

In November 2023, she admitted that one of her sons had lost nearly all the money he invested in cryptocurrencies after he didn't heed her advice.

In January 2025, Lagarde emphatically ruled out the option of including Bitcoin in the reserves of European central banks.

Lagarde dismissed the proposal by Czech National Bank Governor Aleš Michl to study the possibility of investing in Bitcoin. According to Lagarde, the reserves need to be liquid, safe, and secure.

In his debut post, Stanley Druckenmiller, who managed billion-dollar funds in the traditional market, announced that he had become an investor in the fintech startup trade[xyz]. WeWork co-founder Adam Neumann didn’t plan for his family’s control of WeWork to end at his death but instead expected to pass that control to future generations of Neumanns, too, says Business Insider.

The outlet reports that in a speech Neumann gave to employees in January of this year, footage of which it says it has viewed, Neumann is seen saying that WeWork isn’t “just controlled — we’re generationally controlled.” He reportedly goes on to say that while the five children he shares with wife Rebekah Neumann “don’t have to run the company,” they “do have to stay the moral compass of the company.”

According to BI, Neumann even invoked his future grandchildren, telling those gathered: “It’s important that one day, maybe in 100 years, maybe in 300 years, a great-great-granddaughter of mine will walk into that room and say, ‘Hey, you don’t know me; I actually control the place. The way you’re acting is not how we built it,’” he said.

These may sound like more outlandish proclamations from Neumann, who has a flair for the dramatic. (Talking to Fast Company earlier this year, he compared WeWork to a rare jewel, asking, “Do you know how long it takes a diamond to be created?”)

But before WeWork began coming apart at the seams, Neumann had every reason to believe that he could pass power down to his heirs.

#5352. Polymarket Hit by Massive Hack

A massive security breach has reportedly seen nearly 1,000 accounts on the crypto-based prediction market Polymarket drained, with the attack leading to losses of more than $2.6M.

Blockchain analyst Conor Grogan revealed that a total of 995 accounts were hit by the attack, resulting in losses of roughly $2.65 million.

Polymarket has seen 995 accounts drained by a hacker, for $2,654,211.42. Largest losses were 341k and 307k Hacker has converted all funds to POL (most likely to avoid freezing) https://t.co/PjT2QhgBSa

The two biggest losses detected by Grogan were $341K and $307K.

Moreover, the analyst also revealed that the attacker has converted all stolen funds into Polygon's native token (POL). This move might have been made to avoid having the funds frozen.

"If you are a @Polymarket user lock your account. I just got drained $800,000," a trader warned via X.

The trader also claimed that a friend lost another $600K and warned users not to interact with the website.

As noted by blockchain investigator StarPlatinum, the attacker stole roughly $2.68M in just one hour.

The data shows that at about 17:05 UTC, an empty wallet began receiving funds.

At 17:25 UTC, the wallet had amassed roughly $412K.

However, the figure jumped to $2.02M at 17:50 UTC and reached roughly $2.68M at 18:05 UTC.

In total, the attacker has amassed some 28.6M POL tokens, as noted.

So far, it appears that the attack might have occurred due to a hack of a third-party JavaScript component that was embedded in the Polymarket website.

It's not the first time that the popular prediction market has faced a massive hack leading to a multimillion-dollar security breach.

We've identified & fixed an issue impacting our international platform, Polymarket⁠.com. One of our 3rd party providers was compromised, and we have referred this to relevant law enforcement. Anyone who has been impacted will be made whole. Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily halted trading & are working to bring the platform back online.

In June, Polymarket also faced a similar hack. The attack happened when hackers compromised a third-party vendor and injected malicious JavaScript into the frontend of Polymarket.

In total, some $2.94 million was stolen from at least 11 wallets.

Now, Polymarket has reportedly confirmed that the security breach occurred due to a hack of a third-party service provider.

The company also vowed to make every affected user whole. In other words, users who suffered losses due to the attack will be compensated.

#5351. Hackers Target Crypto Users With Fake ChatGPT and Claude Apps

Cybercriminals have been using the hype surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to distribute cryptocurrency mining malware through fake desktop apps that mimic popular AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude.

In a recent report, cybersecurity vendor Check Point Research (CPR) said threat actors have been setting up fake GitHub repositories to advertise fake AI apps like GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus, among others.

The hackers have even set up dedicated GitHub.io sites that promote their fake AI apps and trick victims into downloading malicious files.

According to the CPR researchers, the attackers are using search engine optimization (SEO) manipulation to get their malicious sites to rank high on Google.

One of the most worrisome aspects of the campaign is how the attackers use legitimate software components from OpenAI and Anthropic to mask malicious activity.

The malicious ZIP archives that victims can download feature legitimate digitally signed executable files. These legitimate executables are bundled with malicious DLLs.

Once victims run the seemingly legitimate application, the malicious DLL gets loaded without their knowledge, thanks to the DLL sideloading technique.

This makes it very hard for victims to spot the attack since the malware relies on legitimate software to run its code.

At the end of the day, the attack leads to the installation of XMRig, a cryptocurrency miner that quietly uses the victims' resources to mine digital assets for the attackers.

Interestingly, the malware can also stop mining whenever it senses user activity so that it can evade detection.

In addition, CPR researchers discovered that the malware includes several techniques to make security investigations harder.

For example, it can pause execution for a very long time if it senses that it is not running under the expected executable file.

It also checks the keyboard language setting on a computer before going ahead with the infection.

The first GitHub repository for the campaign showed up in July 2026, and malicious downloads started popping up at the end of August.

At the moment, the payload is a cryptocurrency miner, but researchers have warned that YobaLoader can potentially be used to deploy other types of malware.
