#5320. Exclusive: Numeracle Raises $28M To Keep Legitimate Business Calls From Spam Label

Numeracle has raised $28 million from Edison Partners to help businesses whose calls are incorrectly labeled as spam or blocked by phone carriers, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively.

The McLean, Virginia-based company verifies businesses and links their identities to the phone numbers they use to contact customers. It shares that information with the systems carriers use to screen calls and works to remove incorrect labels.

The financing brings Numeracle’s total funding to $34.8 million since its 2018 inception. That total includes a $6.8 million Series A raised in December 2023, founder and CEO Rebekah Johnson told Crunchbase News in an interview. Edison was the sole investor in the new round. Numeracle declined to disclose its valuation.

The company says it has roughly 4,000 business customers and about 85 employees. It became profitable this year, sooner than Johnson had expected.

Numeracle plans to use its new capital to hire and expand internationally. The company also plans to adapt its business verification tools for use beyond phone calls. For example, Johnson said the company is eyeing messaging, chat apps, marketplaces and AI agents.

Its expansion comes as businesses simultaneously face two related problems. For one,  fraudsters are increasingly impersonating them. Meanwhile, call-screening systems can prevent their own calls from reaching customers.

For example, that could mean a patient ignoring a call from a hospital about an upcoming procedure. For a bank, it could mean a customer declining a legitimate call because the phone displays a fraud warning.

Numeracle charges an annual subscription to monitor and address incorrect spam labels. Customers can also pay a per-call fee to display their business name, logo and reason for calling on a recipient’s phone.

Johnson, an engineer who previously worked in regulatory compliance at telecom provider West, said she recognized the problem while participating in the Federal Communications Commission’s Robocall Strike Force in 2016.

She warned carriers that their efforts to identify unwanted calls would also affect legitimate businesses because the screening systems lacked information about who was calling.

About three months later, she said, a carrier’s federal regulatory counsel called her while she was in her parents’ kitchen.

“Everything you said was going to happen is happening. What do we do?” she recalled him asking.

Johnson said that conversation prompted her to start Numeracle.

She was a newly single mother who had lost her job and used her life savings to start the business. Living on a farm in Grand Bay, Alabama, without internet access, she worked from cafes.

“When you need to feed your children and provide a roof over their head, you’re going to count every penny,” Johnson said.

That experience shaped her spending decisions as Numeracle grew, she said. The company operated for several years before raising its Series A.

Johnson said about 90% of Numeracle’s sales inquiries come through unpaid inbound channels. With the new funding, she plans to spend more on marketing to specific industries, including healthcare.

The company’s customers also include businesses in financial services, home services and higher education, as well as government organizations and charities. Johnson declined to identify individual customers.

Numeracle first checks that a business is real and does what it claims. Once it passes those checks, the company links it to the phone numbers it uses and shares that information with the systems carriers use to flag or block calls.

Other companies can also pay Numeracle to run those checks on businesses they’re considering taking on as customers.

Johnson said Numeracle built its own verification tools because existing services weren’t thorough enough. Fraudsters have an incentive to get through: If Numeracle approves them, their calls are less likely to be flagged as spam.

AI has made it more difficult to tell which businesses are real, she said. Numeracle has encountered fake companies with state registrations, employer identification numbers and supposed employees who have active LinkedIn profiles.

“The scary part for me isn’t necessarily the AI voices,” Johnson said. “It’s actually AI-built businesses.”

She said Numeracle uses AI to help identify those fabrications, though she declined to describe the methods in detail.

Numeracle currently operates in the United States. Johnson said interest from Europe has prompted it to move forward with its international expansion plans, with some of the new funding going toward that effort.

The broader question for the company is whether businesses will pay to use its verification services across other forms of communication. For now, its business centers on a more immediate problem — helping customers recognize a legitimate phone call.

For Lenard Marcus, a general partner at Edison Partners, Johnson’s telecom and engineering experience was one major reason to invest. In an interview with Crunchbase News, he said her industry knowledge helped her build both the product and relationships with companies that could bring it to customers.

He was also drawn to how much Numeracle had accomplished with relatively little funding, describing Johnson as “someone who was frankly doing more with less.”

Customer interviews helped make the case. Marcus recalled one contact center operator who said Numeracle had increased the number of calls answered from 19,000 to 22,000 out of 40,000 calls a month. For businesses trying to reach prospective customers, that increase in conversations could lead to more sales.

Marcus also believes that Johnson’s years in telecom give Numeracle an advantage over newer competitors. In addition to understanding how the different parts of the industry work together, Johnson has used those relationships to get Numeracle in front of large companies, he said.

“She’s sales. She’s engineering, and she’s just a very, very good leader,” Marcus added.

Looking ahead, the investor also sees demand across healthcare, retail, home services and finance, with AI making impersonation more prevalent.

“This is a communications problem, not one for one industry,” he said.

#5317. The Crunchbase Tech Layoffs Tracker

Tech Layoffs Continue In A Week Led By EBay And Electronic Arts

Nearly a dozen tech companies reported a reduction in force in the past couple of weeks, affecting at least 1,790 workers.

The majority of this week’s tally comes from eBay, which reported its second round of 2026 layoffs. According to a report in Reuters, the San Jose, California-based e-commerce giant is trimming its workforce by 1,100, or 9%, in an effort to “simplify operations and shift resources to its fastest-growing areas.”

The gaming sector also ranked high in this week’s count with a pair of companies reporting layoffs. Leading that industry count in the disclosed number of workers affected is Redwood City, California-based Electronic Arts. Per a report in Variety, the software provider is restructuring its studios business, which includes the total shutdown of its BioWare games studio in Edmonton, Canada. Since this is a global cut, it’s unclear how many U.S. workers will be affected.

And, in a workforce reduction that hasn’t made it to the layoff stage, yet, earlier this week Microsoft said it is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 of its global employees. Per a report in Reuters, a source said the Redmond, Washington-based tech giant is making the offer available to staff company-wide, with the exception of its marketing, commercial business and security divisions.

The following companies were added to the tracker this week:

Layoffs during the weeks ended Oct. 28, 2026: At least 1,790 U.S. tech sector employees were laid off or scheduled for layoffs, per a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2025: Around 127,000 workers were let go from U.S.-based tech companies according to our tally.

In 2024: At least 95,667 workers at U.S.-based tech companies lost their jobs in 2024, according to a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2023: More than 191,000 workers in U.S.-based tech companies (or tech companies with a large U.S. workforce) were laid off in mass job cuts.

In 2022: More than 93,000 jobs were slashed from public and private tech companies in the U.S.

This tracker includes layoffs conducted by U.S.-based companies or those with a strong U.S. presence and is updated at least bi-weekly. We’ve included both startups and publicly traded, tech-heavy companies. We’ve also included companies based elsewhere that have a sizable team in the United States, such as Klarna, even when it’s unclear how much of the U.S. workforce has been affected by layoffs.

Layoff and workforce figures are best estimates based on reporting. We source the layoffs from media reports, our own reporting, social media posts and layoffs.fyi, a crowdsourced database of tech layoffs.

We recently updated our layoffs tracker to reflect the most recent round of layoffs each company has conducted. This allows us to quickly and more accurately track layoff trends, which is why you might notice some changes in our most recent numbers.

If an employee headcount cannot be confirmed to our standards, we note it as “unclear.”

A layoff can be either a permanent termination of someone’s employment — usually for cost-saving reasons — or a temporary one because there’s not enough work to justify a full workforce. Tech company layoffs generally fall into the permanent category.

A mass layoff is when a significant number of a company’s employees are cut in a short period of time, often as a result of economic conditions.

Tech layoffs started to surge in 2022 and continued in 2023 and 2024. Companies have given various reasons for conducting layoffs.

Some companies — especially those in the e-commerce sector — nearly doubled their employee headcount to meet consumer demand during the COVID-19 pandemic’s stay-at-home mandates, and later found that they were overstaffed as daily life returned to normal.

Large tech employers such as Salesforce and Google parent Alphabet noted that their post-pandemic layoffs followed several years of rapid hiring fueled by fast growth — between 2019 and 2022, some companies nearly doubled their employee headcount. Some large tech companies also cited slowing sales and fears of a recession as reasons for downsizing.

Venture-backed startups, meanwhile, also cut jobs as a way to cut costs and preserve their cash reserves, as venture funding fell significantly after the peak in 2021. Some startups that ran out of cash and couldn’t raise new funding found themselves filing for bankruptcy or shutting down.

Intel Corp. laid off the largest number of people among U.S. tech employers in 2024, by our count. The semiconductor giant laid off more than 15,000 employees last year.

It was followed closely by electric-car maker Tesla, which cut more than 14,000 roles, and networking company Cisco, with more than 10,000 total roles cut.

In 2023, Amazon layoffs led the numbers with 16,000 roles cut. Layoffs at Alphabet, the parent company of Google, totaled about 12,000, and Microsoft’s layoffs totaled about 10,000 workers in 2023, as did Facebook parent Meta’s layoffs.

Many venture-backed tech startups have also done layoffs as venture capital investment has fallen sharply since the peak in 2021, and falling startup valuations factor into their decisions to conduct layoffs.

Yes, more layoffs are likely coming. While there are signs that the volume of layoffs is tapering, experts we talked to expect job cuts in the tech sector to continue for the foreseeable future as large tech companies and startups continue to battle economic headwinds.

Seed and early-stage startups in particular may continue to conduct layoffs in an attempt to extend their cash runways in a difficult venture funding environment.

Tech layoffs noticeably increased at the start of 2022, ramped up in 2023, waned somewhat in 2024 and have continued in 2025.

Signs that may indicate a company is more likely to conduct layoffs include:

Layoffs declined in 2024 compared to the previous year, but are expected to continue into 2025, although likely not at the level seen in 2023. Startups that need to preserve cash to extend their runways are more likely to conduct layoffs.

Tech layoffs will likely slow when venture capital funding increases and the startup economy stabilizes, as well as when market conditions improve and more startups gain liquidity via IPOs.

Startups that raised capital during the venture funding heyday at inflated valuations in 2021 are more likely to need to conduct layoffs if they’re not able to sustain their previous valuations or growth projections.

Tech layoffs started surging in the 2022 market correction, with an estimated 93,000 U.S. tech workers laid off that year. That figure more than doubled in 2023, with around 200,000 U.S. tech employees laid off, according to our Tech Layoffs Tracker. Layoffs abated again in 2024, with around 95,000 reported tech layoffs.

Keep in mind, many companies don’t report detailed layoffs figures, and some companies continue hiring after cuts for positions deemed more beneficial to the business.

No, according to experts in the sector, who say a sale is unlikely to solve a tech company’s cash-flow issues.

This is especially true as fewer startup M&A deals are happening in the current downturn.

Tech layoffs have hit across departments at many companies.

Many layoffs from the large tech giants were software engineers. Startups tend to be more likely to retain engineers in favor of doing layoffs in their talent and recruiting, marketing and other departments.

Google cut roles in its sales, recruiting, product and engineering teams. Amazon layoffs included jobs in its AWS cloud unit, at its social video platform Twitch, and in its advertising department. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company’s recruiting department would be the first to see job cuts.

#5316. Crypto Stocks Lost Up to 54% in October as Hedge Funds Erased Every AI Stock Purchase Since 2025: Why Did Bitcoin Miners Fall Hardest?

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

Crypto stocks start November after an October that cost them up to 54%, more than six times Bitcoin’s drop, as Goldman Sachs data showed hedge funds sold enough AI stocks in five sessions to wipe out all their net AI buying since early 2025.

That matters for crypto because the biggest losers weren’t the exchanges. They were Bitcoin miners, which have spent two years renting their power and data centres to AI companies and now trade like AI infrastructure.

Cipher Digital (CIFR) fell 53.9% between the September 30 and October 30 closes, and IREN lost 41.4%. MARA and Riot dropped 40.2% and 36.4%. Bitcoin, tracked by BlackRock’s IBIT, fell 8.4% over the same days, and the S&P 500 barely moved.

The exchanges caught up later. Coinbase and Robinhood held up through the hedge fund selling streak, then lost 17% and 16% in the second half of the month, much of it on Friday after the Binance hack and Coinbase’s results.

So were crypto stocks sold as crypto, or as AI?

JUST IN: Hedge funds are pulling money out of US stocks at fastest pace ever

Hedge funds sold AI stocks for five straight sessions, from October 8 to 14, on Goldman Sachs’ prime brokerage data. Most of it was funds dumping shares they already owned, about 3.5 times the pace of new short bets, and roughly $20 billion of tech stock went out over two weeks.

Goldman Delta-One head Rich Privorotsky put the problem in one line: computing demand “can grow exponentially, but the capital available to finance it cannot.”

That line describes the miners. Cipher, IREN, Hut 8, TeraWulf and Core Scientific have all signed deals to host AI computing, and IREN’s AI cloud revenue of $70.5 million overtook its Bitcoin mining revenue of $66.7 million for the first time last quarter.

The selling streak shows who traded as what. From the October 7 close to October 14:

Every miner fell harder than chip stocks in the week hedge funds dumped AI, Cipher more than three times as hard, while Bitcoin hardly moved.

The miners, then the trading venues, then the Bitcoin holders. Over the full month, the order lines up with how much of each business looks like AI or trading volume, and how little looks like Bitcoin itself.

Strategy is the tell. A company that is mostly a pile of Bitcoin fell in line with chip stocks (-14.2%), not with miners, and Circle, which earns interest on stablecoin reserves, fell least of all.

The trading venues had their own problem. Most of Coinbase’s and Robinhood’s losses came after October 14, once the hedge fund streak was over, and Friday alone took 10.6% off Coinbase and 7.2% off Robinhood.

The timing points to AI money for the miners, though it is no proof: Bitcoin’s own 8% slide and a weaker hashprice cut into their mining revenue too.

Discover: Oil Prices Climb Back Above $110 While Crypto Stocks Lose Up to 48% in a Month: Miners Are Falling Even Faster

IREN is the clearest test of the AI trade among crypto stocks, and it reports fiscal first-quarter results on Thursday, November 5. The stock closed Friday at $23.95, down 8.8% on the day, after touching $23.06, its lowest in a year.

The daily chart shows a stock that lost its floor. The July 29 low at $28.93 held through the summer, gave way on October 15, and turned into the ceiling: IREN’s bounce stalled at $28.88 on October 28 and fell the next two days.

May 12 to October 30, 2026: IREN 1D chart. Source: Yahoo Finance (Nasdaq).

Both averages are far above. The 50-day EMA (exponential moving average) sits at $35.64 and the 200-day at $40.82, and the 50-day crossed below the 200-day on September 30, just before the selling began.

For crypto stocks, Thursday is the first chance to see whether AI customers are still paying the miners, or whether October’s selling was right about the capital running out.

#5314. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5313. Jumbo Series A Rounds Hiding The Real Squeeze On Seed Startups

Global startups have closed at least 114 Series A rounds of $100 million or more so far this year, Crunchbase reported in late September, and more than 70% of them went to AI companies. For most seed founders, that headline is a warning.

U.S. startups closed 272 Series A rounds in the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data, about 28% fewer than the 377 a year earlier. Seed held up better, at 984 rounds vs. 1,059. The megarounds hide how few A rounds are getting done.

Seed checks keep growing. The median U.S. seed round was about $3 million last year, 3x its 2018 level, according to Crunchbase. Yet only 24% of companies that raised a $1 million-plus seed in 2023 have moved past seed, and just 16% of the 2024 cohort, down from 55% or higher through 2020.

Uncork Capital‘s Andy McLoughlin told Crunchbase News that Series A investors now expect $2 million to $3 million in ARR, sometimes $4 million, and the time from seed to A has stretched past two years. If a seed won’t carry you to that bar with six months to spare, a smaller round is the better deal.

A bigger seed isn’t required. Take Atomic, a New York-based supply chain planning software company founded in 2023 (and not an MGV portfolio company). It raised a $3 million seed, right at the median, in April 2025, led by Madrona and DVx Ventures, then closed a $12.5 million Series A led by Madrona and Klass Capital about 17 months later.

Funds of $100 million to $500 million typically lead the Series A. Figure out which ones lead at your stage and when their current fund closes, then send the right partners updates for a year before you ask for anything.

The Series A bar is now a revenue bar, which makes it a go-to-market problem first. Most seed companies I meet have a stronger product than sales motion.

At MGV, our work starts with a first session we call Sales Jumpstart: we interview the founders and their team. We then score the company on our proprietary matrix: where it is today, where it should be, and what it needs to become a scalable go-to-market machine.

From there, founders work through workshops on outbound reach, qualification, profiling, the funnel, objection handling, hiring assessment, compensation plans, fundraising, deck building, storytelling and investor intros, with mentoring alongside.

A company at $2 million in ARR with a sales process a new hire can run is a better Series A candidate than one at $3 million built on founder-led deals nobody else can repeat. The founders who make it are already planning for the round after this one.

XRP Ledger (XRPL) took third place in the global ranking of blockchain platforms by the pace of weekly growth in stablecoin capitalization.

According to the official weekly report of the RWA Foundation organization, compiled on the basis of on-chain data from the analytics platform Token Terminal, over the reported seven days, the net inflow of capital into XRPL-based stablecoins amounted to $58.3 million.

The inflow follows a sharp pullback: as of October 22, XRPL's stablecoin capitalization had dropped 13.19% week-over-week to about $999.9 million, as Ripple moved part of its RLUSD supply to Ethereum.

In terms of the volume of attracted funds for this period, XRP Ledger outpaced such blockchain platforms as TON (+$9.6 million) and Polygon (+$9.4 million). Regardless of the current liquidity dynamics, technical testing of the SponsoredAccountCreate update continues in the XRPL ecosystem.

This feature is aimed at reducing corporate costs through fee subsidization: companies will be able to mass-create wallets for their clients without the need for a mandatory freeze of a starting balance of 1 XRP. However, the Sponsor amendment it depends on had only nine validator votes as of October 29, far short of the required supermajority.

The top lines of the global ranking by volume of net weekly capital growth were taken by two infrastructure platforms focused on the corporate B2B segment and automated settlements:

Arc (1st place): The specialized blockchain network Arc, launched by Circle as an infrastructure layer for automated settlements of AI agents and smart contracts, topped the ranking. Over the reported week, the volume of stablecoins in it increased by $252.2 million, which is more than 2.5 times the result of its closest pursuer.

Tempo (2nd place): The second position was taken by the payment blockchain platform Tempo, which recorded a weekly capital inflow of $98.2 million. The Layer 1 network, developed with the participation of fintech giant Stripe and venture firm Paradigm, is focused on commercial merchant settlements. The growth of its indicators was driven by the inflow of liquidity into the network's base stablecoin, Open USD (OUSD).

#5311. Series B Funding Is Up, But Fewer Deals Are Getting Done

More money, fewer rounds. That, in short, is the state of U.S. Series B startup funding in 2026, as venture capital investment continues to concentrate heavily around a handful of AI hotshots.

Crunchbase data shows that so far this year, investors have poured around $48 billion into financings around the Series B stage 1, the highest tally in years. Yet round counts are below year-ago levels and are on track for a multiyear low.

One trend driving capital concentration is a sharp decline in small and mid-sized Series B rounds.

So far this year, less than a third of deals in our sample set 2 were for under $30 million. By contrast, between 2021 and 2025, rounds in this range accounted for about half of deals, per Crunchbase data.

The smallest Series B deals have gotten particularly scarce. This year there were just 26 rounds under $10 million in our sample set.

On the flip side, really large Series B rounds are quite popular.

At least 110 companies have raised rounds of $100 million or more around this stage so far this year. That’s roughly a quarter of all deals.

Of these, the largest by far was a $12 billion round 3 for Prometheus, Jeff Bezos’ physical AI startup that launched last year.

Model developer World Labs, led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li, was tied for next-biggest fundraiser, closing on $1 billion in February. Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics also secured $1 billion in Series B funding across tranches this year, with Sequoia Capital as lead investor.

For  a wider snapshot, below we put together a sample list of more of this year’s biggest U.S. Series B recipients.

Meanwhile, one of the least surprising findings from our analysis of Series B recipients is that it was a heavily AI-focused group.

So far this year, about two-thirds of Series B funding has gone to AI-focused startups, per Crunchbase data. In 2025, by comparison, about half of investment went to companies in AI categories.

AI companies were also heavily represented by round count. So far in 2026, more than half of all reported U.S. Series B deals have been for AI companies.

Overall, the numbers point to a bullish climate for Series B investment, particularly for AI startups with demonstrated traction. The environment looks particularly favorable for companies that have already raised considerable sums at Series A and seed.

Even so, these don’t look like the best of times for startups seeking smaller Series B rounds. Seems like in the current AI-driven cycle, investors are increasingly focused on big checks for high-valuation companies.

Dogecoin has just formed a death cross on its daily chart for the first time since 2026. The 50-day simple moving average (SMA) has crossed below the 200-day SMA, completing a death cross on the daily chart. The last time Dogecoin saw a death cross signal on its daily chart was in November 2025, which preceded months of downward price action.

The development comes only about three weeks after Dogecoin recorded a golden cross on its chart. On Oct. 5, Dogecoin's shorter-term moving average, the 50 DMA, moved above the 200 DMA in a bullish golden crossover.

Krisspax, a Dogecoin community member, highlighted this development in an X post: "We have a death cross on the Dogecoin chart when the 50-day SMA crosses below the 200-day SMA. It's only been about 3 weeks since we had a golden cross, the shortest crossover I've seen for DOGE of this type, stressing the volatility of Dogecoin trading."

The golden cross and death cross signals on Dogecoin's daily chart are unusually close to each other. There is about a 3-week gap between them, indicating a sudden change in momentum.

A golden cross is generally interpreted as a sign of improving medium-term momentum, while a death cross suggests that the shorter-term trend has weakened relative to the longer-term trend.

Dogecoin's price surprisingly rose ahead of the death cross signal, rising for three consecutive days to reach a high of $0.081 on October 29 before momentum slipped.

DOGE sharply fell to a low of $0.074 on Thursday, extending the drop on Friday to a low of $0.072, last seen in August 2026, as the market reacted to the news of Binance's $6.3 billion heist, deemed the largest in crypto history.

Total liquidations reached $1.68 billion in the last 24 hours, according to CoinGlass. Long positions, bets that prices would rise, accounted for the majority of the total at $1.43 billion.

Support is expected next at $0.069, while resistance stays near $0.086, around the daily moving averages.

#5309. Bitcoin Sellers Take a Week of Losses Below $80,000 as Strategy and Strive Keep Buying: Will $75,000 Hold?

All reviews, research, news and assessments of any kind on The Tokenist are compiled using a strict editorial review process by our editorial team. Neither our writers nor our editors receive direct compensation of any kind to publish information on tokenist.com. Our company, Tokenist Media LLC, is community supported and may receive a small commission when you purchase products or services through links on our website. Click here for a full list of our partners and an in-depth explanation on how we get paid.

Bitcoin (BTC) sellers booked their longest run of daily losses since mid-August last week, Glassnode said on Monday, November 2, as Strategy and Strive added 935 BTC between them, though Strategy spent three times as much buying back its own preferred stock.

Strategy bought 811 BTC for $65.5 million, at an average of $80,846, taking its stash to 849,327 BTC. The same filing shows $208.2 million going into STRC, the preferred stock Strategy sells to fund its purchases, which has been trading just under its $100 face value.

Strive bought 124 BTC for $10 million at $80,526 each, chief executive Matt Cole posted, bringing it to 43,124 BTC. For the first time, part of it was paid for by selling SATS, Strive’s own preferred stock.

Both companies bought above today’s price. Bitcoin trades at $77,948, below the $80,000 line where Glassnode says sellers have been accepting losses all week.

In August and September, the same kind of selling marked the bottom. So are sellers close to done again, or is the treasury buying too small to matter?

bitcoin:native sellers have been taking losses below $80k.Last week brought the longest run of daily net realized losses since mid-August.The August and September loss clusters both formed at the local lows. A hold above $75k would fit that pattern. pic.twitter.com/DCjbNfhoT7

A pattern that has twice marked a low. Glassnode tracks realized profit and loss, the gain or loss on each coin when it moves, against the price it last moved at. Since the October 29 Binance hack sent BTC under $80,000, the losses have outweighed the profits almost every day.

The firm’s chart, titled “Profit Taking Is Slowing Down,” marks the earlier loss clusters:

The logic is simple. Sellers who accept a loss are usually the ones who bought high and gave up, and once they are out, there are fewer coins left to dump.

“A hold above $75k would fit that pattern,” Glassnode wrote.

Two clusters in three months is a short record, though, and the August one came at a much lower price. The pattern only holds if buyers show up, which brings in the companies.

Its filings don’t say, but the price points to one reason. STRC is built to trade close to $100, and it closed Friday at $99.13. Strategy’s November 2 filing shows it bought back 2.09 million shares for $208.2 million, about $99.52 each.

That has become the bigger job. Over the last five weekly filings, Strategy spent $974.9 million on STRC and $137.8 million on BTC.

The board has topped up the buyback program by about $1 billion since mid-October, leaving $748.6 million to spend. Strategy now holds 849,327 BTC at an average cost of $75,451, about 3% below the current price.

Mostly with cash it already had. Strive’s 124 BTC came a week after it bought 6,182 BTC for $511.4 million, so the pace has dropped sharply.

The new part is SATS, Strive’s preferred stock. Its sales program was used for the first time, and all of the week’s program proceeds came from it rather than from ASST common shares, which fell 28% between October 21 and 30.

Cole also put Strive’s amplification ratio at 62.7%. That is its debt and preferred stock against the value of its BTC, so the lower the price, the higher it climbs. At Friday’s $76,764, Strive’s 43,124 BTC were worth $3.31 billion.

Discover: Bitcoin Rebound Faces a Test in Strategy’s STRC Funding

So far, it has held higher. BTC trades at $77,948 on Binance, down 0.5% on the day, and has stayed above its October 30 low of $76,326 for three days. That low sits right on the 200-day EMA (exponential moving average) at $76,510.

Both treasury companies bought above here, at $80,846 and $80,526, which is roughly where the 50-day EMA now caps the price at $80,287.

August 5 to November 2, 2026: BTCUSDT 1D chart. Source: Binance.

For Bitcoin, the test is the one Glassnode set: if $75,000 holds while the loss-takers finish, last week will look like August and September again.

#5308. Sector Snapshot: Travel Tech Funding Heads Toward Multiyear Low Despite AI Push

Travel demand appears to be holding up, but at the same time, investor appetite for travel tech startups has cooled. Even a wave of startups promising to improve travel with AI hasn’t managed to reverse the funding slowdown, a review of Crunchbase data shows. Whether uncertainty over how AI will reshape travel planning and booking is contributing to that pullback remains an open question.

Startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion this year through the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data. The largest funding recipients span a wide range of categories including hotel management software, travel booking platforms, alternative accommodations and corporate events. The mix also includes electric aviation, travel finance and insurance, and consumer hospitality businesses, reflecting a broad definition of travel tech.

The broad trend: Investors are making far fewer bets on travel startups than immediately before and after the COVID-19 pandemic, Crunchbase data shows. This year could be the lowest since at least 2018 when it comes to dollars raised and deal count.

AI is a recurring theme among the largest funding recipients, with many using it to perform functions such as automating hospitality operations, personalizing bookings and streamlining travel planning.

The numbers: In the first three quarters of 2026, startups in the travel tech space have raised $2.2 billion globally across just 302 funding rounds, Crunchbase data shows. That’s down fairly significantly so far from the $3.7 billion raised in 2025. Deal volume is on track to fall for a third consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Funding and deal volume in recent years remain far below past levels. In 2021, for example, funding in the sector topped $12 billion. That’s a bit surprising considering that so much travel was halted in the midst of the COVID-19 pandemic. But even prior to the pandemic, funding and deal totals were much higher — totaling $9.4 billion across 1,277 deals in 2018 and $10.4 billion across 1,190 transactions in 2019.

Even travel industry researcher Skift noted the funding downturn in a recent newsletter, saying: “Though it’s too early to say whether this is a long-term market movement, it’s a clear sign of the times.”

Interestingly, several of the year’s largest deals involved startups headquartered outside of the United States.

The year’s largest funding recipient through the third quarter was Mews, which raised a $300 million Series D in January led by EQT Growth, with participation from Atomico, HarbourVest Partners, Kinnevik, Battery Ventures and Tiger Global Management. The Amsterdam-based hospitality software company helps hotels manage reservations, payments and operations, and says it plans to expand its use of AI agents to automate workflows. The financing valued the company at $2.5 billion.

Chinese electric aircraft developer Aerofugia raised about $144 million in February in a financing led by CITIC Securities, joined by New Alliance Capital, Vertex Ventures China and other investors. Chengdu-based Aerofugia, also backed by automaker Geely, develops electric passenger aircraft that take off and land vertically, often called flying taxis.

Montreal-based Stay22 secured a $122 million minority growth investment from Summit Partners in February. The startup uses AI to help publishers, creators and event organizers turn their audiences’ interest in travel into bookings and affiliate revenue.

Home-swapping platform Kindred announced an $85 million Series C led by Index Ventures in February. The San Francisco-based startup operates a members-only network where travelers exchange stays in one another’s homes. Its announcement also included a $40 million Series B co-led by New Enterprise Associates and Figma CEO Dylan Field, bringing the combined funding disclosed that day to $125 million.

Another large deal went to Paris-based Naboo, which announced a $70 million Series B in February led by Lightspeed Venture Partners with participation from Notion Capital, Isai and Ternel. The company uses AI to help businesses source venues, organize corporate events and manage related purchasing and payments.

Several travel startups have found buyers in 2026, including companies developing AI tools for planning and booking trips. Amadeus acquired corporate travel AI assistant SkyLink in February, while Expedia acquired AI trip-planning startup Layla in July. Both deals illustrate a trend of established travel companies buying startups to expand their AI capabilities.

Expedia also completed its acquisition of venture-backed Tiqets, a booking platform for museums, attractions and experiences, in February.

On the IPO side, a potentially prominent prospective exit fell through. Travel experiences platform Klook withdrew its planned U.S. offering in October after having filed last November.

Still, the downturn in startup funding and dearth of IPOs in the sector hasn’t affected one of the bigger now-public players in the space. Corporate travel booking and expense management platform Navan has seen its stock rise nearly 60% this year. Formerly called TripActions, it began trading on Nasdaq under NAVN in October 2025. Its stock closed at $27 on Oct. 28, up about 58% this year from its Dec. 31 closing price of $17.08. It was also 8% above its $25 IPO price, meaning much of this year’s gain recovered from losses following the listing.

#5307. Not Just Ledger: Karpeles Warns of Tampered Trezor Devices

The ex-CEO of the now-defunct Mt. Gox, Mark Karpeles, has flagged the potential compromise of Trezor hardware wallets sold by Southeast Asian reseller CryptoBilis, indicating that the recent supply chain attack on Ledger devices is not an isolated case.

"Ledger n'est pas la seule. @Trezor devices sold by CryptoBilis were also implanted," Karpeles said in an Oct. 30 post on X.

In his post, Karpeles advised customers who bought Trezor devices from CryptoBilis from March 2026 onwards to immediately transfer their cryptocurrency to new wallets with new recovery phrases.

He also offered to manually review potentially compromised devices, saying that he would be willing to cover the shipping fees if customers wished to get their wallets checked.

Karpeles's alert follows Trezor's confirmation that its security team was made aware of a credible report of a suspected hardware implant in a Trezor Safe 5 device.

As detailed in Trezor's Oct. 30 announcement, the device in question was acquired through the online marketplace Tokopedia in Indonesia in August 2026.

The report on the suspected device was received by Trezor on Oct. 28, and a video interview with the customer was conducted.

That said, Trezor said it hasn't checked the device in question in person to verify the report.

The report states that the suspected compromised device has an extra board between the main board and the screen.

The extra board has a cellular module and an antenna that can receive data from the device, such as the wallet's recovery phrase.

Afterwards, the data can be sent via a mobile network when the hardware wallet is plugged in.

This suspected modus operandi is similar to the highly advanced hardware implants previously found in Ledger devices sold by CryptoBilis.

In fact, Ledger's investigation into suspicious fund losses involving the reseller began on Oct. 9. Later, it was confirmed that some Ledger devices had been physically tampered with.

On the same day, Trezor decided to cut ties with CryptoBilis as an authorized reseller.

Four devices bought by CryptoBilis customers have been checked by Trezor, but no signs of tampering have been found so far.

According to Trezor, no CryptoBilis customers have reported losing funds in connection with the suspected Trezor implant.

Despite this, Trezor recommends that affected customers create a completely new wallet instead of just restoring their existing recovery phrases on other devices.

While mainland China maintains a strict ban on cryptocurrency transactions, the American platform Solana Foundation has made a major step in the region by signing a strategic agreement with a local licensed issuer in Hong Kong, Anchorpoint Financial Limited.

The partnership launches the HKDAP stablecoin for retail payments and tokenized assets — this is the project's first direct collaboration with a public blockchain foundation.

The issuer Anchorpoint is a consortium of Standard Chartered Bank (Hong Kong), telecom operator HKT and Animoca Brands, which received the FRS01 license from the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA).

Integration with Solana provides instant issuance and redemption of the asset, opening a legal banking gateway for retail and for trading real-world assets (RWA).

The deal rests on Hong Kong’s Stablecoins Ordinance, which took effect on August 1, 2025: any issuer of a fiat-referenced stablecoin must hold an HKMA license, fully back the token with high-quality liquid reserves and redeem it at par.

Since the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the US dollar within a 7.75–7.85 band, HKDAP effectively becomes another dollar-linked instrument, but one issued in a separate jurisdiction outside direct US regulation.

Solana's infrastructure is ready for this: according to rwa.xyz data as of October 30, 2026, the total RWA volume on the platform stands at $18.89 billion, of which $14.13 billion (around 75%) is made up of stablecoins with a monthly transfer volume of $370.94 billion across 13.56 million addresses.

Consolidating its position, Solana Foundation is joining Hong Kong's government program OASES, opening a local office and rolling out the TAP tokenization program together with PwC.

This infrastructure creates a legal track for big capital. While mainland China tests the digital yuan exclusively within state-controlled pilot zones, Hong Kong provides clear rules of the game for private business.

As a result, Standard Chartered and its partners get a fully legitimate settlement instrument, and the international market gets direct access to Hong Kong dollar liquidity via the Solana blockchain.

#5304. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

MetaMask is facing fresh questions about its future after Consensys launched a new institutional settlement network targeting banks, asset managers and financial market infrastructure providers.

Consensys unveiled Sovereign Network Interoperability at Devcon, introducing infrastructure designed to coordinate transactions across independently operated financial networks. Can MetaMask maintain its position as institutional blockchain adoption accelerates?

The new Sovereign Network Interoperability platform aims to help institutions settle securities, exchange currencies, and move collateral across separate blockchain networks.

Its bridgeless design keeps assets on their original ledgers while coordinating transactions between approved counterparties. Consensys says the system uses cryptographic verification to reduce reliance on additional trusted intermediaries.

The platform targets four major financial workflows, including securities settlement, wholesale payments, collateral mobility, and tokenized fund transactions.

Consensys plans to support Ethereum-compatible networks and protocols such as the Ethereum Economic Zone and Inter-Blockchain Communication. Canton connectivity is also planned.

The launch builds on Consensys’ existing institutional infrastructure, including Linea, Hyperledger Besu and Teku. The company is positioning itself as a technology provider for financial institutions seeking private, always-on blockchain settlement.

#5302. More Money, Fewer Checks: These 3 Charts Show The Divide Behind VC’s Record Funding Year

Startup capital is both more abundant than ever this year and yet scarcer. That contradiction has become increasingly visible in 2026 when analyzing Crunchbase data, and the trend continued through Q3.

Our data shows that despite record venture capital spending in 2026 — nearly $680 billion through Q3 — investors are writing fewer checks to seed and early-stage companies, the businesses one typically thinks of when we talk about startups.

One of the best ways to visualize this dichotomy is by looking at how much of the record global venture funding this year went to funding rounds across different tiers: less than $100 million, $100 million to just under $1 billion, and $1 billion and more.

As illustrated above, the funding surge this year is concentrated in those largest rounds, while the smaller-round market has essentially flatlined since 2023.

The massive surge in billion-dollar-plus rounds in Q1 and Q2, of course, was thanks to record-setting financings for OpenAI and Anthropic. But it’s not just those two companies concentrating capital at the top. About one-third of Q3 funding went to just 27 companies raising billion-dollar-plus rounds.

In North America, the largest startup market, deal counts have trended downward over several years, even as venture investment soared.

In Q3, reported deal counts in North America fell 16% year over year and 14% quarter over quarter, reaching the lowest quarterly total since 2023, even as North American funding dollars jumped 50% year over year to $92 billion. The contraction is concentrated in seed and early-stage deals — North American late-stage counts actually increased year over year.

Series B is a particularly stark illustration of the dollars-up-but-deals-down trend. Series B marks the stage when startups are maturing: they typically show some growth and traction but still have plenty of upside potential. But while dollars invested in U.S. startups at the Series B stage hit a multiyear high so far this year, deal count is on track to hit a multiyear low.

It’s a similar story among seed and Series A startups, with money concentrating into larger rounds even as deal count dips.

Anthropic, the biggest venture-backed private company of all, is slated to go public this month in a potential $2 trillion IPO, offering a prominent test of public investors’ appetite for the companies driving this venture boom.

A strong public-market reception could reinforce venture investors’ willingness to finance enormous AI bets, while a disappointing debut could put unicorn valuations under pressure.

But neither outcome guarantees that funding will reach a wider pool of startups. The real measure of a broader startup recovery we’ll be watching: whether deal counts start to rise alongside the dollars.

#5301. Ledger CTO Sounds Alarm Over New Cryptographic Threats to Bitcoin

Two new cryptographic breakthroughs raise concerns over the future of Bitcoin (BTC) and other cryptocurrencies, according to Ledger Chief Technology Officer Charles Guillemet.

According to Guillemet's Oct. 30 post on X, a recent study shows that it might be easier to break the mathematics behind elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC), which is how Bitcoin is secured.

“Thought it was a bad week for crypto? You may have missed the real news,” wrote Guillemet.

Elliptic-curve cryptography works by making it practically impossible to solve the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem.

So far, the best general method to solve it has been Pollard’s rho algorithm. Its computational cost increases exponentially with key size.

Now, the researchers have presented a subexponential algorithm that might in theory solve it more efficiently.

There is a big caveat. It relies on another claim by OpenAI researchers that requires further investigation.

The new algorithm doesn’t put current cryptographic schemes at risk, Guillemet insisted.

The best attacks for popular curves, like secp256k1 for Bitcoin, NIST P-256 and Ed25519, are still based on Pollard’s rho.

The new one would only be more efficient for hypothetical curves of very large sizes. For now, it’s just theoretical.

The second breakthrough is a big advance in the efficiency of quantum computing attacks on elliptic-curve cryptography.

Guillemet referenced a public research project, ECDSA.fail, aimed at improving the efficiency of quantum computing attacks against elliptic-curve digital signatures.

Researchers managed to reduce the estimated quantum circuit cost by about 70% relative to what Google previously reported, the Ledger executive explained.

Current estimates put the cost at about 0.91 billion in the logical-qubit-times-Toffoli-gates metric, down from 2.99 billion in Google’s figures.

What’s more important is that the French quantum computing company Alice & Bob has published a new paper estimating that it’s theoretically possible to break Bitcoin's secp256k1 cryptography using fewer than 30,000 physical cat qubits in about an hour.

The same paper estimates that factoring RSA-2048 would require 22,593 cat qubits and take about 3.14 days.

Such a quantum computer does not exist, so there is no immediate risk to Bitcoin, Guillemet noted.

However, these findings are a reminder of how the estimated resources needed to break common cryptographic schemes keep shrinking.

The daily XRP/USD chart shows lower highs, weakening momentum and a break below several moving averages. After September's rally toward $1.60, XRP started to correct, and the recovery attempts since then never turned into a lasting uptrend. That left it open to more selling.

Now the latest drop has pushed XRP below its major moving averages, the 200-day near 1.36–1.37 included, which keeps the bearish picture intact.

The nearest support is around $1.20–$1.22. The latest intraday lows are there, and $1.20 is a round number besides.

If XRP breaks below $1.20 and the break is confirmed, selling pressure could speed up toward $1.15 and then the $1.10 support area. If sellers keep control, the $1.00 psychological level could become a longer-term target.

On the upside, the first resistance is between $1.28 and $1.30. Reclaiming it would be an early sign that selling is easing. Above that, 1.33–1.37 is tougher, since several moving averages meet there.

RSI has fallen to the low 30s, which signals strong bearish momentum and puts XRP close to oversold. Oversold readings can lead to short rebounds. They don't prove the bottom is in, though.

Volume was also higher on the way down, giving the breakdown more weight.

Short term, XRP stays bearish while it trades below $1.30. A recovery above that level could let buyers try for the 1.35–1.40 resistance zone, but as long as XRP is under the major moving averages, sellers keep the upper hand.

And if the $1.20 region fails, the correction could stretch toward $1.15 and possibly $1.10. Until buyers reclaim the key resistance levels, the downside risks remain high.

Ethereum (ETH) has extended its slide, dropping below $2,300 as sellers took more control. On the daily chart, ETH trades near $2,222.59 after a sharp rejection from the 2,350–2,400 resistance region.

It's been a big drop from the October peak near $2,800. The series of lower highs and lower lows points to a bearish trend, and that comes after a strong recovery in August and September.

Buyers may try to hold the nearest support at 2,170–2,200. A clear break below it could speed the selling up toward $2,100 and then the $2,000 threshold.

To ease the downside pressure, Ethereum needs to win back $2,300. There's more resistance near $2,350, and a sustained move above $2,450 would be a more convincing sign that buyers are returning.

RSI sits near the lower edge of its neutral range, in line with steady selling. ETH is getting close to oversold, but the indicator hasn't confirmed a bullish reversal.

Heavy trading volume during the decline only adds to the worries about sentiment. The wider crypto sell-off also came at the same time as reports of a major Binance security incident, which added uncertainty across digital assets.

#5298. China’s Largest Startup Deal Ever Lifts Global Venture Funding To $59B In October

Global venture funding in October totaled $59 billion, a 45% jump from a year earlier, per Crunchbase data, in large part due to a record-setting deal for China’s DeepSeek. The company’s $15.9 billion funding round marked the largest-ever venture deal for a Chinese company ever, and came in the same month that two other frontier labs raised blockbuster Series A rounds totaling at or close to $1 billion.

The bulk of October’s venture funding was invested in the two leading countries for startup investment, with companies based in the U.S. and China raising $28 billion and $20.6 billion last month, respectively. The last time more than $20 billion was invested in China in a single month was June 2018, when Ant Group raised $14 billion in its Series C funding.

Funding concentrated in seven companies that raised billion-dollar rounds, accounting for just over 40% of October’s venture funding. These large amounts were invested in frontier labs, manufacturing, energy, semiconductors, prediction markets and spend management software. Private equity led much of this funding, along with a few multistage venture firms including Sequoia Capital, Index Ventures and Lux Capital.

DeepSeek’s $15.9 billion raise at a valuation of $90 billion marked the largest private funding by a Chinese tech company on record. The deal places DeepSeek among the Top 10 most highly funded private companies. It also makes it the second most highly valued Chinese company after ByteDance, and the third most highly valued private frontier lab after U.S. companies Anthropic and OpenAI.

DeepSeek wasn’t the only Chinese frontier lab to raise big in October. Moonshot AI, a rival open-source lab, reportedly reached a $50 billion value in October, making it the 11th most valuable private company on The Crunchbase Unicorn Board. The startup has also reportedly confidentially filed to go public on the Hong Kong stock exchange.

Massachusetts-based manufacturing startup Re:Build raised the second-largest funding deal last month, a $2.1 billion round. The company partners with industrial companies and innovators from the product design phase to large-scale production and says it has 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity.

Other large rounds last month went to Axiom, which raised $2 billion for power and grid capacity build out for data centers; spend-management platform Ramp, which raised $1.85 billion and said its ARR has reached $2 billion; open-source semiconductor company Tenstorrent, which says it  raised a $1.5 billion Series E funding and recently moved its  headquarters to Silicon Valley from Canada; prediction market Kalshi, which raised a $1 billion Series E; and frontier lab Flapping Airplanes, which raised a $1 billion Series A.

A further eight companies raised rounds north of $500 million last month. They spanned industries ranging from frontier labs, robotics, legal and chips, to agentic AI and healthcare. Among the most notable was TypeSafe AI, which says it raised an $870 million Series A funding on the heels of rapid developer adoption of its decision model Jev.

A total of 66% of global funding was in AI-driven companies in October, with semiconductor companies gaining market share this past month.

The U.S. IPO market was slow in anticipation of Anthropic’s November IPO. The offering could surpass even SpaceX’s record-setting June listing that raised $85.7 billion.

On the M&A front, at least nine venture-backed companies were acquired for more than $1 billion last month, including Uber’s acquisition of 19-year-old ezCater for $2.3 billion.

With two months remaining, 2026 has already set records for acquisitions, IPOs and funding rounds across major venture markets. October extended that momentum, but also highlighted how concentrated this cycle has become: Seven companies accounted for more than 40% of global funding, while AI-driven businesses captured two-thirds.

The question heading into year-end is how widely that momentum will spread, as Anthropic prepares to list in what could be the largest IPO of all time.

The data contained in this report comes directly from Crunchbase, and is based on reported data. Data is as of Nov. 2, 2026.

Cohere is targeting a $5 billion funding that was announced in October, without reporting an initial or final close. This funding was not included in the October monthly totals.

Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year.

Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price.

Seed and angel consists of seed, pre-seed and angel rounds. Crunchbase also includes venture rounds of unknown series, equity crowdfunding and convertible notes at $3 million (USD or as-converted USD equivalent) or less.

Early-stage consists of Series A and Series B rounds, as well as other round types. Crunchbase includes venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $3 million, and those less than or equal to $15 million.

Late-stage consists of Series C, Series D, Series E and later-lettered venture rounds following the “Series [Letter]” naming convention. Also included are venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $15 million. Corporate rounds are only included if a company has raised an equity funding at seed through a venture series funding round.

Technology growth is a private-equity round raised by a company that has previously raised a “venture” round. (So basically, any round from the previously defined stages.)

#5296. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5295. Why November's +80% History Is a Statistical Flaw for XRP Holders

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

XRP's 15.7% drop in October has brought the token to the most unpredictable crossroads of the year. Historical data from thirteen years of observations promise the market harsh November volatility. However, behind the optimistic figures of past years lies a serious methodological flaw capable of disorienting investors amid the current pressure.

The main trap for the market is the asymmetry of returns. According to Cryptorank, XRP's average November gain is an impressive +80.2%, but this figure is completely distorted by two isolated anomalies: a surge of +531.9% in 2013 and a rally of +281.7% in 2024. The month's median, a negative -10%, reflects reality much more accurately.

Historically, in most cycles, XRP closed November in the red. The fourth quarter, which so far consists of October alone, is already down -16.3%, in line with the asset's seasonal tendency toward correction that the averaged statistics mask.

The median is not a perfect guide either: thirteen observations are a small sample, and the market structure has changed. Since spot XRP ETFs launched in the US in mid-November 2025, the token has had an institutional demand channel that did not exist in earlier cycles.

Mathematical pessimism is reinforced by the real balance of power on the market at the end of October. The XRP price has fallen below the key support line of $1.30 and is trading around $1.25–$1.26, marking a local downtrend.

All the upward momentum built on investors' expectations has faded, opening the way for profit-taking by short-term players. Notably, the October decline follows a 48% gain in the third quarter, XRP's best Q3 in four years, which suggests that at least part of the current pressure is profit-taking after the rally rather than seasonality alone.

The situation is aggravated by an inevitable influx of supply amid a liquidity shortage. On Sunday, November 1, a scheduled unlock of 1 billion XRP from Ripple's escrow wallets will take place.

It is worth noting, however, that the escrow unlock is a routine monthly event that has followed the same schedule since 2017, and Ripple typically returns 600–800 million XRP to new escrow contracts. The real net addition to circulating supply is therefore closer to 200–400 million XRP.

Even so, against the backdrop of thin liquidity, this volume is enough to put additional pressure on the price, as it will enter the market simultaneously with macroeconomic pressure and the aftermath of the recent wave of forced liquidations of long positions worth more than $1.29 billion, caused by a security incident at the Binance exchange.

At the same time, the wave of liquidations has partially cleared excess leverage from the market. If funding rates stay negative and open interest does not recover, the bearish scenario may be capped by a short squeeze, which would make a retest of $1.30–$1.32 more likely than the statistics suggest.

#5294. XRP Reserves on Binance Hit Lowest Level Since 2022

As the broader crypto market continues to face intense selling pressure due to the prolonged market volatility seen over the past weeks, XRP appears to be seeing rising demand instead.

While its price is also struggling amid the market downturn, onchain data from crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant shows that more tokens are leaving major exchanges instead, which could be interpreted as intense buying.

The data shows that XRP reserves on the world's largest exchange by volume, Binance, have dropped to their lowest level since December 2022.

As of October 30, Binance has seen its XRP reserve fall to 2.47 billion XRP from the 2.69 billion XRP it recorded on October 28, marking a sharp decline in its holdings in just two days.

This signals rapid accumulation from traders as it marks a decrease of about 8.18% in the amount of XRP available for sale on Binance, with over  220 million XRP withdrawn in just a two-day period.

While decreases in exchange reserves simply mean a reduction in the amount of XRP readily available for trading, it potentially reduces immediate selling pressure if demand remains steady, thereby providing a bullish outlook for the token.

Further data shows that the decrease in the XRP exchange reserve on Binance has coincided with falling XRP balances on several other major crypto exchanges, including Bybit and Bithumb.

The data shows that reductions seen on these exchanges were smaller compared to Binance, as Bybit's XRP reserves dropped from 306 million to 286 million XRP during the same period.

Bithumb, on the other hand, also recorded a decrease of 10 million XRP, with its reserves falling from 1.847 billion to 1.837 billion XRP, down approximately 0.54% during the same days.

While this indicates a broader reduction in exchange-held supply and XRP has remained volatile despite the shrinking supply, it is important to note that lower balances do not always mean that investors are accumulating XRP, which could be the reason XRP has yet to react to the trend.
